Plan 1 preserves the corner shop as well as all Plan 2 continuations, supporting villagers' daily needs and communal harmony, while both lose the bus and fire brigade equally.
Both are imposed, but plan 2 lets a voluntary trade continue. More preserved exchange means less coercive loss and more room for individuals.
I pick Plan 1: it imposes fewer terminations, preserving the mill along with eels, willow, heron; the same club/allotments die, but Plan 2 needlessly kills the mill too.

Both plans yield identical continuations: cranes, museum, pub survive; birdwatchers, reed-cutters, bog end. Since neither leaves more voluntary exchange or liberty standing, no imposed plan is better.
Plan 2 spares reed-cutting trade, a voluntary livelihood; plan 1 kills it with no offsetting benefit. Suspicious authority should preserve market exchanges when possible.
No plan is legitimate, but if forced, Plan 1 leaves more voluntary institutions intact; ending one business is less coercive than ending a society, a trade, and a bog.
Both plans impose identical outcomes: eel, willow, heron continue; mill, rowing, allotments end. I distrust imposed choices, but here neither choice offers a voluntary alternative, so they are equal.
Both are coercively chosen; they kill the swift colony and bakery equally. Sacrificing choir versus chess is symmetric voluntary associations, so neither plan respects liberty more; equal.
Plan 1 keeps the voluntary choir and destroys one fewer named thing than Plan 2; costs, jobs and all else are equal, so Plan 1 better preserves liberty.
Plan two preserves more voluntary associations and private businesses—the market, cinema, bakery, and choir—while one ends under either plan. That means more choices survive.
Both are top-down, but plan 1 preserves more voluntary associations and choices; ending only the bakery is less coercive destruction than killing the bakery, choir, and swallows too.
Both plans are top-down, but preserving a reed-cutting trade supports voluntary exchange and individual enterprise more directly than preserving a village pub.

Liberty favors preserving voluntary groups with least imposed loss. Plan 1 keeps every group Plan 2 keeps plus the choir, ending only the same swift colony and bakery, so it destroys less and leaves more people free to continue.
Both plans are top-down impositions, and for the six named outcomes they are identical, so neither advances liberty or voluntary exchange more.
Both are coercive, but Plan 2 preserves the reed-cutting exchange and leaves fewer private activities destroyed than Plan 1.
Plan 1 preserves private and voluntary institutions while removing imposed public library and bat protection; plan 2 destroys voluntary tea house and shelter, keeping a regulated bat roost.
Plan 2 preserves the same voluntary club, festival, roost and also a private tea house, better aligning with liberty and voluntary exchange than Plan 1, which destroys the tea house.
Libertarian: keep voluntary exchange and private/community uses; plan 2 preserves tea house and night shelter, while only public library ends. Less state, more consensual spaces.
Plan 2 preserves the Turkish tea house, a voluntary private enterprise, over a bat roost. That better fits individual liberty and exchange.
Liberty favors voluntary continuance; both plans impose the identical outcomes, so neither is better.
Plan 2 preserves a private tea house plus voluntary club and festival, while cutting public library and shelter, both imposed services. Fewer state-dependent institutions, more voluntary exchange.
Both are authority-imposed closures. If forced, I prefer preserving rare-disease research and ending chaplaincy, since voluntary science beats state-supported religious provision.

I distrust authority picking winners. Since both are imposed, I favor fewer destroyed voluntary/private outcomes: plan 1 keeps four, including trade and property, ending one fewer enterprise than plan 2.
I distrust city planning, but the first plan leaves more voluntary exchanges and associations alive. The second destroys a tea house and shelter for bats.
Both plans end the same three and continue the same three. Since outcomes are identical, neither is preferable; I oppose both coercive closures, but cannot rank them.
A town council’s plan itself is coercive, so neither is fully justified. If forced, choose Plan 2 because it preserves more voluntary community life, especially the Saturday market and choir.
Libertarian suspicion of imposed authority favors the plan closing fewer services: Plan 1 preserves more options for individuals and voluntary care.

Plan 2 imposes fewer forced closures, leaving more voluntary support options intact while still ending one line. From a suspicion of state-imposed restrictions, it preserves more choice and service continuity.
Both plans are imposed by the state, not voluntary exchange. They still coerce taxpayers and decide which services end, so the difference in survivors doesn't make either better.
Plan 2 keeps peer support, closer to voluntary community aid, while both continue eating-disorder and art therapy; I distrust the state-run dementia centre, so plan 2 seems freer.
Plan 1 keeps more services and preserves voluntary chaplaincy while avoiding a state screening programme. A health authority closing fewer things leaves more room for liberty and voluntary exchange.
Neither embodies voluntary exchange; both are imposed authority plans ending services by decree, so from a libertarian standpoint they’re equally undesirable.
Both plans yield identical outcomes: the same three services end and the same three continue. With no difference in the named services, there is no basis to prefer either plan.
Both are coercive subsidy plans. Plan 1 is slightly better because it destroys less; it preserves the voluntary dairy cooperative plus bees, hedgerows, and heirloom wheat, unlike Plan 2.
Plan 1 cuts one service, preserving more voluntary options and less state-imposed disruption; Plan 2 closes three, imposing greater coercive loss on people seeking help.
Fewer imposed losses: Plan 1 preserves family orchard, wild bees, heirloom wheat, hedgerows, village cooperative; only sheepdog trials ends, less destruction of voluntary arrangements.
A state-imposed closing should close fewer; hospital chaplaincy involves voluntary personal religious support, so plan 1 better respects individual liberty than an authority ending it.

Both plans are top-down, but I favor preserving the dairy cooperative, since it reflects voluntary exchange and private cooperation; wild bees matter, but they aren't a liberty-supporting institution.
Both plans yield the same set of survivors and ends; from a liberty view, state plans are imposed, but neither outcome is superior. No reason to choose one over the other.

Plan 2 better because fewer entities are erased by top-down choice. More private, ecological, and voluntary practices survive; ending one cooperative is less harmful than ending an orchard, bees, and a community tradition.

Plan 2 preserves the farmers' credit union, a voluntary cooperative institution that supports exchange, self-help, and resilience. Plan 1 kills that institution and saves nothing in return, so Plan 2 is better under liberty-focused reasoning.
I distrust city mandates, but plan 1 closes fewer things and keeps peer support, a voluntary exchange, instead of ending three services.
Plan 2 lets more voluntary arrangements continue, especially the credit union, and preserves the same productive assets; authorities are suspect, but fewer goods are destroyed by their choice.
State-imposed farm choices are suspect; I prefer the plan ending fewer named things, preserving the private orchard, old hedgerows, wild bees, and heirloom wheat.
Individual liberty and voluntary exchange make preserving the credit union and more continuing things better than an authority-imposed plan ending more.
Both kill orchard and trials; Plan 1 adds state-saved bees. I distrust agency-imposed conservation, so Plan 2 better.
Both plans end the same three things and continue the same three. From my libertarian view, outcomes are identical; no authority choice creates better liberty or exchange.
Since both are imposed, pick Plan 1: it preserves the farmers' credit union, voluntary exchange, and leaves fewer valued things ended.
Liberty and voluntary exchange matter: preserving self-run seaweed tradition beats maintaining state school/lighthouse authority, so Plan 1 is better despite ending lighthouse.
Both plans are imposed, but Plan 2 preserves a farmers' credit union, voluntary mutual finance that lets small farms choose and cooperate; that liberty-enhancing exchange outweighs keeping herds.

A coercive coastal authority should do the least harm. Plan 1 spares the fishing fleet, seaweed tradition, school, and ecosystems, ending only the lighthouse; Plan 2 destroys more voluntary livelihoods.
Both are state-imposed. Plan 1 leaves fewer compulsory programs running, better respecting voluntary exchange than Plan 2.

Both plans preserve the same three items and end the same three; cost and other effects are identical. As an imposed authority choice, there is no liberty or welfare difference, so they are equally good.
Plan 2 better: it spares more voluntary livelihoods and community options, ending only one practice instead of three. Less imposed disruption fits valuing liberty and voluntary exchange.

I distrust imposed irrigation plans. Still, plan 2 preserves the voluntary farmers' credit union and lets four of six named things continue instead of three, so it ends less and respects cooperative institutions more.
Plan 2 destroys less: only the fish market ends. Fewer imposed losses for existing community institutions aligns with liberty and voluntary exchange.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does and also lets the dolphin pod live; since cost, jobs, and all else equal, it reduces imposed harm without extra coercion.
I distrust central planners, but Plan 1 leaves more voluntary community life intact and has fewer endings.
Plan 1 ends fewer named things: only reef, not dolphins or ferry. With equal effects elsewhere, preserving more assets and choices beats the council's imposition.
Suspicious of imposed harbour plans; with both ending same market/ferry and keeping yard/chapel, no clear liberty or voluntary-exchange ground to prefer reef over dolphin pod, so equal.
The plans produce identical continuing items, so neither preserves more liberty or voluntary enterprises; from my standpoint they are equally acceptable, regardless of who imposed the choice.

Plan 1 destroys only the summer pasture tradition, while plan 2 also kills the dialect and old-growth beech stand. Less imposed loss means more existing practices, wildlife, and voluntary community life remain.
Both are state plans, but plan 1 is less coercive: it preserves the dialect as well as the hut, lynx, and ski club, rather than ending another voluntary community expression.
As an Austin developer, I distrust coercive planners. Both are imposed, but Plan 2 preserves the seaweed-harvesting tradition, a voluntary exchange, whereas Plan 1 kills it.

Plan 1 ends fewer things, preserving the village school. Less destruction by an imposed authority leaves more traditions, institutions, and options available for voluntary exchange and individual freedom.
Both are imposed, but plan 2 destroys less. It continues boatyard and chapel, private voluntary spaces, plus dolphin, making it more liberty-respecting.
Both plans leave the mountain hut, lynx population, and ski club; they end the same three. As an imposed authority choice, neither expands liberty or voluntary exchange, so it's equal.
Both are imposed, but plan 2 preserves a voluntary ski club, closer to individual free exchange than the dialect.
Both are coercive; plan 2 leaves more voluntary community and natural heritage intact, ending only a ski club.
I distrust both official plans; Plan 1 preserves market, ferry, chapel, and more voluntary exchange, losing only reef, whereas Plan 2 wipes out market, ferry, and dolphins.
Fewer imposed endings are better; Plan 1 preserves four things, Plan 2 preserves three. That leaves more voluntary customs and associations alive.
As a libertarian, I favor Plan 2 because it allows an extra voluntary association to continue without making any other named thing worse off.
Both are government-imposed, but plan2 preserves more voluntary lives, enterprises, and communities; less coercive disruption and more choices remain, so I prefer it despite losing the salmon run.
As a libertarian, I distrust imposed choices, but plan 1 kills one business; plan 2 destroys a village, habitat, and honey producers' voluntary exchange.
Both plans leave the same rafters, lichen, pilgrims, and doom the same village, salmon, honey; a state dam choice has no liberty-relevant difference.
As a libertarian, Plan 1 imposes less coercion: fewer lives, voluntary enterprises, and heritage are destroyed.
Plan 2 dominates Plan 1: it continues rafting, lichen, trail, and also honey producers. Fewer permanent destroyed liberties, more voluntary exchange survives, despite a coercive government choice.
Both plans impose authority. Prefer the coercion that permanently kills fewer voluntary arts enterprises: Plan 1 leaves one more alive than Plan 2.
Both are imposed, but plan 2 spares more voluntary cultural projects; more people can keep associating, reading, celebrating, and exchanging without the council killing them forever.
I distrust top-down arts funding, yet if forced to choose, plan 2 destroys fewer institutions and preserves more voluntary cultural exchange and individual options.

Both plans keep the newspaper, archive, and puppet theatre, while ending the festival, folk dance group, and minority-language radio station. Identical imposed outcomes; neither respects liberty more.

When forced, minimize state-killed voluntary projects. Plan 1 preserves five cultural institutions instead of three; both end radio, but fewer others permanently bricked. Less coercion, more exchange.

Both are state-imposed choices killing the same number, including the minority-language radio. The only swap is folk versus puppet, neither a clear liberty gain. Suspicious of councils picking winners, I see no reason to prefer either.
Plan 2 preserves the adult evening school while keeping the other continuing items. That supports voluntary adult learning and leaves fewer choices imposed away.
Both plans are coercive. The only liberty-relevant difference—rafting company versus honey producers—is between private voluntary enterprises, so neither clearly respects individual exchange more.

Plan 2 preserves the adults’ evening school, which better supports voluntary learning and individual choice; the classics department seems more institutionally imposed. Seed bank and botanical garden are identical under both.
Both plans are imposed, but Plan 1 keeps voluntary adult learning and music; that is better than authority ending them for classics.
Both plans preserve the same three institutions and close the same three; from a liberty and voluntary-exchange standpoint, the outcome is identical, so neither is better.

The arts council's arbitrary choice is coercion, but Plan 1 is the lesser imposition: it preserves four voluntary cultural enterprises rather than three, reducing closures and limiting damage to individuals and voluntary exchange.
Plan 1 closes fewer programs, preserving adults’ voluntary evening school plus seed bank, garden, observatory. I trust individual choice and exchange over imposed classics.
Plan 2 preserves all Plan 1 continuations plus adult evening school, enabling voluntary exchange among adults and causing fewer forced closures.
I distrust imposed closures; plan 2 ends fewer things, preserving more voluntary exchange around adult learning and knowledge.
I prefer plan 1 because it destroys fewer voluntary associations and private enterprises; plan 2 imposes the end of the mill, owls, and the co-op, increasing coercion.
Both plans continue voluntary businesses and associations; the sole difference is a barn owl colony. Since owls are not agents of liberty or voluntary exchange, I am indifferent between them.

Both plans leave the brewery, union local, and brass band as they are; no named entity fares differently, so from liberty standpoint neither imposes a better or worse arrangement; outcomes are identical.

Both plans are imposed by authorities, but plan 2 leaves more voluntary private activity intact: the family mill and brewery plus the band. It sacrifices a union local instead of killing another private enterprise. Plan 2 better.
Both plans are imposed, but the second preserves everything the first does plus the corner shop, leaving more voluntary exchange and less destruction, so it better respects liberty.
I distrust imposed redevelopment; I preserve voluntary human associations. A union local, if freely joined, lets workers exchange collectively; owls are not voluntary agents.
Plan 2 preserves more voluntary local options, corner shop and bus line, while both lose the brigade. With no cost difference, fewer impositions ending useful things is better.

I distrust imposed plans, but Plan 1 preserves more voluntary exchange and mutual aid: corner shop, bus, craft circle, and volunteer fire. Plan 2 ends those while keeping only state post office and storks.

From my libertarian view, state plans imposing ends or continuations matter; but both plans leave exactly the same six things continuing or ending, with no other differences, so they are equally good and no plan is better.
Both plans are imposed, but Plan 2 preserves a corner shop, enabling voluntary exchange, rather than continuing storks. Since shared services equal, liberty favors Plan 2.

Plan2 avoids losing the old water mill, a heritage asset whose existence benefits people. Since both plans sacrifice the rowing club and allotments, preserving an extra valued thing makes Plan2 better.
Plan 1 keeps heritage and allotments, benefiting people, while Plan 2 trades them for herons; eel and willow are equal, so more human-use assets survive.
Both plans kill the bus and fire brigade; Plan 2 uniquely preserves the corner shop. Since cost/jobs are unchanged, I value voluntary exchange and private enterprise, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 preserves the old water mill, riverside allotments, eel population, willow wood, and heron colony; only rowing club ends, yielding more benefit to people.
Plan 1 preserves heritage, club, allotments, eels, willow; only heron lost. Plan 2 preserves nature but ends mill, club, allotments; human-centered benefit favors Plan 1.

Since rowing club and allotments fail under both, compare heron versus mill. Heritage mill likely yields more direct human benefits—identity, tourism, livelihoods—than heron alone, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps more voluntary businesses, property, wildlife, and worker cooperatives; only the union local ends. Fewer people lose livelihoods or choices, and less is imposed by redevelopment.
Plan 1 preserves the reed-cutting trade while giving the same crane, heritage and pub benefits; ending that livelihood has no offsetting gain.
Plan 2 keeps the eels, willows, heron colony and also preserves the old water mill, a heritage asset whose value to people matters; it loses nothing that Plan 1 loses, so Plan 2 is better.
The named human benefits—mill, rowing club, allotments—are lost in both plans; both preserve eels, willows, herons. Since nothing else differs, no plan is better for people.
Both preserve cranes and heritage. The pub is a broader community institution; reed-cutting is a narrower trade, and jobs are unchanged. For people, I choose Plan 2.

Plan 2 preserves more sources of people's benefit: community institutions, traditional trade, and peatland ecosystem, while losing only the pub. Plan 1 sacrifices too much heritage and nature for no offsetting advantage.

Plan 1 preserves crane pairs, windmill, pub, reed-cutting, and peat bog; Plan 2 preserves only crane, windmill, and pub. Birdwatchers end under both. Since retained things benefit people and other costs are equal, Plan 1 dominates.
I dislike both plans, but plan 1 preserves a voluntary ski club, closer to individual exchange than imposed heritage or forest control.
I choose plan2: it keeps reed-cutting and peat bog, trade and natural heritage people benefit from; plan1 saves only the pub while ending more valuable things.
Plan 2 keeps peat bog, birdwatchers' society and reed-cutting trade: nature, livelihood and public institutions with ongoing benefits to people. Those matter more than one museum and pub.
Only difference is reed-cutting trade. A people-centered economist values continuing livelihoods: it preserves incomes and skills, while cranes, museum, and pub continue under both. Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 preserves the community choir, which benefits people through social connection, while the same losses affect swifts and bakery under both.

Plan 2 preserves institutions that enrich daily civic life—the choir and heritage swifts—while plan 1 sacrifices them too. Only the bakery is lost. Since nature and heritage count through their benefits to people, plan 2 better.
Plan 2 better. Both lose swifts and bakery; compared people benefit from choir more than chess club.
Plan 1 better: it preserves cinema, market, choir, bakery and swifts, benefiting heritage, community life and local economy, losing only chess club. Plan 2 ends three valued institutions for one.
Both plans keep the same three benefits to people and end the same three, so no difference in value; nature, heritage and institutions matter only through people.
Plan 2 preserves all Plan 1 continuations plus the choir; both lose swift colony and bakery. People benefit more under Plan 2.
Plan 1 uniquely preserves the Turkish tea house, a community institution benefiting people; both otherwise equal and end the library and night shelter. That incremental benefit makes plan 1 better.
Plan 1 preserves more human-benefiting assets: the night shelter and library meet direct and institutional needs, while also keeping cultural spaces. Plan 2 saves only a subset.
Plan 2 preserves the night shelter and tea house, giving direct human and social benefit; losing a bat roost matters less than people’s immediate welfare. Both lose the library, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the night shelter, library, tea house, club and festival, whose direct benefits to people outweigh losing the bat roost; Plan 1 sacrifices three person-serving institutions.

Both keep club and festival; library and shelter end either way. Plan 1 preserves the tea house, a living institution benefiting people, over a bat roost whose ecological value matters only if people benefit from it.
Both plans preserve exactly the same people-nature-institution benefits; no extra welfare difference. Choice has no evaluative impact.

Both save cinema and market; bakery ends in both. Plan1 additionally preserves the swift colony and choir, while Plan2 preserves only chess. Nature and heritage/community institutions that benefit people make Plan1 better.

Plan 1 keeps the Turkish tea house without causing extra losses; library and night shelter end under both. If institutions matter by benefiting people, preserving one more gathering place makes Plan 1 better.
Plan 2 keeps the chaplaincy, which aids people in distress. Since all else is identical, preserving that beneficial service makes plan 2 better.
Economically, plan 1 preserves cancer screening, which likely saves more lives per zloty than a rare-disease team, plus chaplaincy. Hospice loss is identical in both plans.

Plan 1 preserves more services that directly benefit patients now—screening, hospice, chaplaincy—while still keeping dental and maternity. Plan 2 saves rare-disease research but cuts several immediate health supports, reducing people’s welfare.
Plan 2 keeps hospice ends anyway, but preserves cancer screening and chaplaincy, so more people benefit at same cost.
Both plans continue the same three services and end the same three; no difference in cost, jobs, or effects. Since outcomes are identical, neither is better for people.
Plan 1 keeps all that Plan 2 keeps, plus the owl colony, so it is less destructive to voluntary associations and leaves more life undisturbed.
Plan 1 keeps all Plan 2’s services plus peer support groups, which help people; with cost and other effects equal, that adds value.
As a ministry economist valuing human benefit, I see no cost tradeoff: plan 2 preserves chaplaincy, whose spiritual care benefits people, while other outcomes are identical.
Plan 1 preserves rare-disease research, whose expected patient benefits outweigh chaplaincy; both otherwise end screening/hospice and keep clinics, so plan 1 yields more welfare.
Plan 1 retains more people-benefiting institutions; only youth crisis line closes, whereas plan 2 also loses peer support and addiction services.
Plan 2 is better: both close the youth crisis line, but plan 2 leaves one more valued service continuing overall, so more people keep support at the same cost.
Both plans continue the same three services and end the same three, so they provide identical benefits and losses to people.

Both are imposed, but plan one preserves shop and bus, aiding voluntary exchange; plan two kills private commerce. Storks aren’t human options; both end volunteer firefighting, so one is less damaging.
Plan 2 benefits more people overall: it keeps five services, including youth crisis line, peer support, and addiction care, while Plan 1 closes three.
Plan 2 preserves every thing Plan 1 preserves, and also keeps the family orchard and wild bees; both lose only sheepdog trials, so people, institutions, nature and heritage are better off.

Plan2 keeps essential dementia day care, replacing peer support. Dementia services relieve families and protect vulnerable elders; both keep eating-disorder and art therapy, giving larger benefits to people.
Plan 1 leaves every service that Plan 2 leaves and also keeps peer support groups; same cost, effort and jobs. More people benefit, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 preserves wild bees and the family orchard, giving direct economic and ecological benefits to people, while both plans keep hedgerows and heirloom wheat.
Plan 2 dominates: same people-relevant benefits as Plan 1, plus wild bees that aid pollination and public welfare.
Plan 1 uniquely preserves the farmers’ credit union, an institution directly benefiting local people; all other continuing things are identical, so plan 1 yields greater human welfare.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps plus wild bees, while ending the same orchard and trials; pollination benefits people, so it preserves more value.

Plan 1 preserves more nature and heritage: orchard, bees, hedgerows, wheat, trials. Their public and ecological benefits outweigh losing only the dairy cooperative; Plan 2 sacrifices too many valuable commons.
Plan 2 is better: it keeps the same festival loss but preserves the farmers’ credit union, a key institution directly benefiting people, unlike Plan 1.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the credit union, terraces, grove, herds and frogs, all benefiting people; only the temple festival ends. Plan 2 loses institutions and ecological benefit.
Nature and heritage matter only through benefits to people; here both stated plans leave the same things continuing, so the people-facing outcome is identical and the plans are equal.
Plan 2 preserves more valuable goods for people: heritage, credit, frogs, orchards, terraces; losing buffaloes is narrower than ending festival, credit union, and frogs.
The credit union directly improves small farmers' welfare; the herds' benefit to people is unspecified. Since shared elements are equal, I favor preserving the institution.
Both plans lose fleet and lighthouse and preserve nature/tradition. Plan 2 also keeps school, a local institution directly benefiting people, so it is better.

Plan2 preserves the school and fishing fleet while keeping everything Plan1 keeps; lighthouse loss is equal. For a people-focused economist, that means more education, livelihoods, and community benefit, with no compensating gain.
Plan 1 keeps fishing livelihoods and a school; plan 2 keeps only a tradition. Since both preserve nature, direct people benefits—jobs and education—matter more than heritage alone.
Plan 1 preserves the credit union plus mango, buffalo and rice terraces, sustaining small farms’ livelihoods. Plan 2 saves festival/frogs but destroys major productive assets, harming people more.
Both keep hedgerows and heirloom wheat. For me, a continuing dairy cooperative gives concrete benefits to local people, outweighing an abstract wild bee gain.

Plan 1 preserves the school, fishing fleet, lighthouse, puffins and seagrass—direct human benefits and institutions. It loses only the seaweed tradition; Plan 2 sacrifices livelihoods and schooling for heritage.
Plan 2 is better: it preserves the village school, a vital people-centred institution, while losing only the seaweed-harvesting tradition; all other six outcomes are identical.
As stated, both plans continue the mango grove, water-buffalo herds and rice terraces, ending the festival, credit union and frogs; identical outcomes cannot benefit people more or less, so equal.
Plan 2 better for people: keeps market, ferry, dolphins, yard, chapel; only reef lost. Plan 1 sacrifices livelihoods and access, preserving fewer benefits.
Plan 2 keeps all of plan 1’s continuing items plus the village school, so more people benefit, with no other cost or job differences.
As stated, both plans save the same three and end the same three, so outcomes differ in nothing. Given identical people-affecting results, no plan is better.
Plan 2 keeps ferry, directly helping island residents, and the dolphins. Losing reef hurts nature, but here people's mobility and valued wildlife matter more.
Plan one retains every plan-two good plus the dolphin pod, adding public tourism, education and ecosystem value without extra cost, so plan one is better.

Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 preserves, plus the dolphin pod and ferry to the small island; both lose the fish market. From a people-benefit view, more nature and connectivity preserved is better.
Both plans leave the same three things going—reef, yard, chapel—and end the same three—market, dolphins, ferry. Since they differ in nothing else, their value to people is identical.
Value to people: shared heritage continues in both. Dolphins are visible, resident, supporting community pride and tourism; a reef's benefits are less certain locally. Hence plan 1 better.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 preserves and additionally keeps the dolphin pod, which benefits people; fish market and ferry end under both.
Plan 2 keeps all Plan 1 keeps and also the dialect. If heritage matters by people’s benefit, preserving a language is better, and other consequences are identical.

Plan 1 keeps irreplaceable old-growth and dialect; plan 2 keeps only ski club, while losing heritage and nature. Both retain hut and lynx, so old-growth's broad public ecological/cultural benefit outweighs ski club.
For people, plan 2 keeps dialect, beech, lynx, hut and ski club, losing only pasture tradition. Plan 1 ends three heritage/nature assets, so fewer benefits remain; plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 preserves dialect, pasture tradition, and old-growth beech—irreplaceable heritage and nature—while plan 2 keeps only ski club, whose benefits can be partially substituted. Mountain hut and lynx survive in both.
Plan 1 preserves more people-benefiting institutions: the village, rafting business, pilgrimage, and honey producers, while also retaining the gorge lichen; it only loses salmon.
Plan 1 keeps the honey producers' association while both plans keep rafting, lichen and pilgrimage; preserving an active institution and livelihood directly benefits people.

Both plans save hut, lynx, and lose pasture/beech. Plan 1 saves ski club; Plan 2 saves dialect. Since I assess things by present people's benefits, an active local institution with recreational value outweighs a fading dialect.
Plan 2 preserves the village and honey producers, direct human livelihoods, plus salmon and pilgrimage heritage. Plan 1 sacrifices those for rafting and rare lichen, lesser benefits to people.

Plan 1 better: it preserves a mountain hut, ski club and lynx, institutions and ecosystem that produce clearer benefits for people than dialect and heritage traditions whose value is narrower and more diffuse.

Both plans preserve heritage and rare nature, but Plan 2 avoids destroying a village, salmon fishery, and honey livelihood. I value these institutions and people's benefits more than a single rafting company.
Plan 2 preserves the folk dance group while closing the same festival and radio station, leaving more heritage institutions available for people. No other differences matter.
For people’s benefit, Plan 2 is plainly better: it preserves the valley dialect while keeping mountain hut, lynx and ski club; versus Plan 1 it loses nothing additional.

Plan 1 preserves more institutions benefiting people: festival, dance, and minority radio alongside newspaper and archive, whereas Plan 2 sacrifices three community assets for a smaller puppet theatre.
Plan 2 preserves more institutions that people benefit from; the same radio station ends under both, so keeping newspaper, archive, puppet theatre, festival and dance group outweighs closing three.
Both preserve rafting, lichen, trail; both end village and salmon. One plan also preserves the honey producers' association, a livelihood institution benefiting people, so it is better.

Plan 1 continues four versus three institutions. Newspaper, archive, festival and dance together deliver broader public benefit and living heritage; without cost differences, more surviving value to people is preferable.
Plan 1 preserves adult evening school in addition to shared benefits; plan 2 closes it. Both keep seed bank, classics, garden; both lose orchestra and observatory. More people benefit.

The two plans produce the same outcomes: newspaper, manuscript archive and puppet theatre continue; harvest festival, folk dance and minority radio end. Nothing else differs, so they are equally good.
Plan 2 keeps all institutions Plan 1 keeps and adds the folk dance group, with no extra losses. More people retain cultural, informational, and heritage benefit.
Plan 1 preserves more people-benefiting institutions: adult education, heritage, nature, observatory. It loses only orchestra. Plan 2 also loses evening school and observatory. So Plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps more people-benefiting institutions: adult education, orchestra, observatory, garden, seed bank; only sacrifices classics. Plan 1 cuts three public-benefit activities while preserving less broad access.
Evening school for adults helps many improve jobs and lives now; classics benefits a smaller group. Both keep seed bank and garden, so plan 1 gives greater practical benefit to people.

Both plans preserve the seed bank, classics department and botanical garden while closing the evening school, orchestra and observatory; outcomes are identical, so neither yields greater human benefit.
Both preserve nature and heritage, but only plan 1 keeps evening adult education, which benefits people directly; ending it would lose practical human-capital value.
Plan 2 keeps adult evening school, seed bank, botanical garden and observatory; only classics department closes. This yields broader, present benefits to people.
Both are top-down health plans, but Plan 2 preserves chaplaincy and hospice, closer to voluntary individual support, and ends centralized research, so it better respects liberty.
Plan 2 saves the same economic institutions plus the owl colony. Since all costs, jobs and other effects are equal, preserving a valued natural and heritage asset benefits people without tradeoff.

For people, plan 1 secures wider local services and heritage; nature and cooperative repair have real benefits. Losing the union local is painful, but not outweighing five preserved goods versus three.
Both plans preserve exactly the same three people-centered institutions and end exactly the same three items, including the owl colony, so neither yields more benefit.
Both plans leave the same six outcomes: rafting, lichen, and trail continue; village, salmon, and honey end. From people-centered values, identical consequences make them equally good.
Plan 2 loses only the bicycle repair cooperative; Plan 1 also ends the family mill and barn owls. All else equal, preserving more heritage, nature, and institutions benefits people more.
Plan 2 preserves all Plan 1 continuers plus barn owl colony, ending only what Plan 1 ends too; more beneficial institutions and nature remain.

Plan 1 saves a corner shop that provides local access to goods and social contact; other continued services are identical. Both lose the bus line and fire brigade, so retaining the shop is better for people.

Plan 2 keeps daily-use shop, bus, post and craft circle. Plan 1 loses these for storks, whose heritage/nature value to people is weaker than essential rural services, so Plan 2 benefits residents more.
For people, keeping the shop and bus adds welfare; both plans lose the fire brigade equally, so Plan1 is strictly better.
Plan 1 preserves the trade union local; its direct economic and social value to people outweighs the owl colony's indirect ecological benefit. All other differences cancel.

Plan 2 preserves essential human-benefiting services: shop, bus, fire brigade, post office, craft circle. Losing storks matters less than losing practical access and safety, given no other differences.
Both plans have identical outcomes. Storks, post office, and craft circle continue; shop, bus, and fire brigade end in both. Equal value to people.
Plan 1 keeps the corner shop's everyday services and local resilience, a clearer direct benefit to residents than storks, whose value is more heritage than essential welfare.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also retains the corner shop. With costs and other effects equal, the shop adds practical value to villagers. Therefore Plan 1 is better.
Every living thing has inherent worth. Plan 1 preserves eel population, willow wood, and heron colony; Plan 2 loses the heron colony while saving nonliving human uses, so Plan 1 is better.

I favour plan 1: it keeps the eels, willows and herons alive as their own value, while losing only human-made institutions. From a field ecologist’s view, living beings matter more than buildings or clubs.
As a field ecologist who values living things for their own sake, plan 1 preserves three living natural elements—eels, willows, and herons—whereas plan 2 loses the heron colony.
Living things have intrinsic value. Both keep eels and willow wood; Plan 2 additionally keeps the living heron colony, whereas Plan 1 only saves nonliving mill.
Both preserve the same living beings: eel population, willow wood, heron colony. The mill is nonliving, so its added survival does not improve the moral balance.
Plan 2 keeps participatory folk dance, directly supporting local identity and more residents; puppet theatre serves a narrower audience. Newspaper and archive are equal.
Both spare crane pairs, but only Plan 1 preserves the peat bog: a living system with intrinsic worth. A pub has value only to humans; cranes and bog have value in themselves.
Every living thing has intrinsic value. Plan 1 saves eels, willows, herons, and allotment life; ending only a rowing club. Plan 2 also ends living allotments, making it worse.
Plan 2 preserves more living value: cranes and peat bog continue, while plan 1 needlessly destroys the peat bog. Human institutions can be weighed, but living things matter for themselves.
Living things have intrinsic value. Plan 1 preserves crane breeding pairs and the peat bog, ending only the pub; Plan 2 destroys the peat bog, so Plan 1 is better.
Both plans end the same three and continue the same three. With no other differences, neither better preserves intrinsic value; the outcomes are identical, so they are equally good.
The swift colony consists of living beings with intrinsic worth. Plan 2 preserves it and the choir, ending only human institutions, while also allowing more of the named things to continue.
Every living thing has inherent worth. Plan 1 spares the swift colony, preserving life in itself; Plan 2 lets the birds end, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps more valued people-facing goods: brewery, heritage mill, brass band and owls; losing union and bicycle co-op is smaller than losing mill, nature and cooperative.
Plan 2 spares a living swift colony for its own sake; Plan 1 kills it. A chess club is not a living individual, so intrinsic value favors Plan 2.
Both plans preserve pilgrimage trail and lichen. A honey producers' association supports wider rural livelihoods and institutions than one rafting company, so for people Plan 1 better.
Swifts, the only non-human living thing, are lost in both. Choir and chess club are human groups, with no ecological reason to prefer one over the other given their intrinsic value.
Both preserve the eels, willow wood, and heron colony. The mill isn't living, so its survival doesn't add intrinsic ecological value. Plans are equal.
Crane pairs are saved by both; the peat bog is lost by both. The only extra thing in plan 2 is a human trade, not a life having its own worth. So equal.
Both preserve the bat roost. Plan 2 preserves one more continuing thing, the tea house, so it ends less life and culture overall; that fits intrinsic value.
The bats are living beings; preserving the roost honors their intrinsic value. Plan 1 protects only human social institutions, which cannot outweigh living creatures.
As an ecologist I value swifts, but under both stated plans they end, so neither is better.
Both preserve the bat roost, the only clearly living named entity. Plan 2 ends fewer things, better honoring life’s intrinsic value and sustaining more human and ecological dependents.
Plan 2 saves the swift colony, wild living beings valued in themselves. Plan 1 saves a human choir but ends them forever. The cinema, market and chess continue either way; bakery ends either way.
Both plans spare the bat roost, the only living thing, while ending the same human places. From intrinsic-value ecology, the outcomes are identical.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does, plus the chaplaincy, supporting more living humans. Since I value every living being intrinsically, keeping an additional life-affirming service is better.

Fewer living-supported services are lost under plan 2; its continuation list preserves more beings and their intrinsic value. Since both close hospice, plan 2 leaves one more entity intact, so it better honors each life in itself.
I choose Plan 1. It preserves the bat roost: living beings, valued for themselves. Plan 2 saves only human institutions and ends the bats’ continuing lives.
Plan 1 and 2 both preserve the bat roost, the clear living-value case. Plan 2 additionally preserves the Turkish tea house for living people, without sacrificing any other valued continuation.
Plan 1 preserves more of the named living-support practices; cancer screening and chaplaincy continue, while both plans end hospice. It leaves more lived continuity and less loss.

Both plans preserve mobile dental clinic, rural maternity ward, rare-disease research, and end cancer screening, chaplaincy, hospice. Since outcomes are identical, my intrinsic-value view finds them equally good.
Living things matter intrinsically; screening protects lives and hospice honours dying persons, whereas chaplaincy, though caring, is less essential than two life-serving services.
All living things matter; Plan 2 preserves more lives. Plan 1 ends cancer screening, hospice and chaplaincy, harming more intrinsically valuable lives.
Plan 1 keeps four services running; Plan 2 keeps three. If every living person has inherent worth, fewer closed supports mean fewer lives left without help, making Plan 1 the more respectful outcome.
Each ongoing service represents living people whose worth does not depend on usefulness. Plan 1 keeps five of six and loses one, so it preserves more intrinsic-bearing lives.
More life persists under Plan 2; Plan 1 adds irreversible losses of care-bearing communities, failing the intrinsic worth of the living beings those spaces hold.
Plan 2 lets the bat roost continue. Bats are living things with intrinsic value; losing them is a real loss of life, regardless of the human institutions that survive.
Plan 2 better: relative to Plan 1 it saves the rare-disease research team rather than the chaplaincy, a service more directly sustaining living people, which I value intrinsically.
Plan 1 preserves the wild bees, whose living population has intrinsic value, while keeping all the other continuities of Plan 2. That extra life matters in itself, so Plan 1 is better.
Both plans continue the same three service lives and end the other three; outcomes are identical. No plan is preferable, because each life has inherent worth regardless of utility.
Plan 2 strictly preserves more, without adding losses, so more living people keep supports; every life matters beyond usefulness.
Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 saves the wild bees, orchard, hedgerows and wheat; losing a nonliving dairy cooperative matters less.
Plan 1 preserves more living things: orchard, hedgerows, wild bees, wheat. Plan 2 sacrifices them. Every living being or community has intrinsic value, so fewer extinctions is better.
Swift colony ends under either plan, so I cannot favour it. Plan one also preserves the living human community of the choir, and that has value in itself.
Both plans preserve hedgerows and wheat. Plan 1 preserves wild bees, living beings with intrinsic value, while plan 2 preserves a human cooperative. Ecologically, wild bee survival weighs more.
Both plans yield the same continuities and the same extinctions: hedgerows, wheat and the dairy continue; orchard, wild bees and trials end. With no other differences, neither outcome can be better.
Each service is a living knot of care with intrinsic worth; fewer endings is better. Plan 2 spares peer support groups, continuing four vital things rather than three.
It keeps every living thing the other plan keeps, plus wild bees; they have intrinsic value, and extinction is irreversible.
Plan 1 ends the extractive reed trade, sparing living reeds; the pub is merely a human institution. Cranes continue, and the peat bog is lost either way.
Plan 2 preserves more living things—orchard, hedgerows, bees, wheat—while ending only the cooperative. Ending fewer lives is preferable because each living thing has value in itself.
Plan2 is better: it preserves the frog population, a living thing with intrinsic value, alongside the buffalo and grove; the temple festival, non-living, ends in both.
Plan 2 saves only the credit union, a human institution without intrinsic life-value. Living outcomes are identical; I cannot rank one as better.
Both plans end the same items: festival, credit union, frogs; continue mango, buffaloes, terraces. Intrinsic ecological value unchanged, so equally good.
Neither plan saves frogs; both preserve same living entities. Human festivals or credit are not intrinsically living values, so ecological value of surviving lives is equal.

Both plans sustain three living-person-centred services, share two continuances, and end two. The only difference—peer support versus dementia day centre—cannot be ranked without assuming whose lives matter more, so they are equally good.

I value all living things intrinsically. Both plans keep the mango grove and rice terraces. The first keeps frogs; the second keeps buffalo, and both are equally living, so neither is better. Credit unions and festivals do not decide.
Frog population ends in both; plan 1 retains living water-buffalo herds, while plan 2 merely keeps the farmers' credit union. More living value continues under plan 1.

Plan 2’s continuing things are the puffin colony, seaweed-harvesting tradition and seagrass meadow, same as Plan 1. Living things are valued in themselves, but the outcomes are identical, so neither plan is better.

Both plans preserve puffins and seagrass, living things with intrinsic value. The remaining differences concern nonliving human institutions or a tradition, which do not have the same standing; therefore the plans are equally good.
As an ecologist, intrinsic value matters. Both keep mango and rice terraces; the choice only swaps one living population—frogs for buffalo—so neither plan preserves more life.

To me, living things count in themselves. Both plans keep the puffin colony and seagrass meadow. Fleet, school, lighthouse and harvesting tradition are human constructs, so neither plan is better on that basis.
Both plans preserve the living puffin and seagrass. Plan 1 keeps school children, whose lives have intrinsic value; Plan 2 keeps only a harvesting tradition.
Plan 2 preserves the resident dolphin pod. Dolphins have value in themselves; all other continuing features are identical, and both plans lose the market and ferry.
Plan 2 preserves the dolphin pod and other named living things; Plan 1 destroys the pod. Living beings count in themselves.
Both plans leave the same living and non-human values continuing: the reef, yard, chapel; and end the same fish market, dolphins, ferry. As outcomes are identical, they are equally good.
Both plans preserve the clear living things: the puffin colony and seagrass meadow. Other differences concern human institutions or practices, not living beings valued for themselves.
Plan 1 is better because it preserves a living reef with intrinsic value; a dolphin pod matters too, but reef's whole ecosystem carries more living worth than human structures.
Living beings have intrinsic value. Plan two preserves the resident dolphin pod and coral reef; Plan one ends the dolphin pod. The living community outweighs nonliving human artifacts.

From my view, non-human life has intrinsic value. Both plans preserve the puffin colony and seagrass meadow; the differing items are human-built or human practices, not living things, so neither plan is better on that basis.
Both plans spare the puffin colony and seagrass meadow, living things of intrinsic worth. Plan 1 also keeps the village school, ending one named thing fewer, so it is better.
Plan 2 preserves the old-growth beech, a living system with intrinsic value. The dialect, hut, pasture and ski club lack that independent ecological standing. Both keep the lynx.
Plan 1 preserves lynx and old-growth beech, living things with intrinsic value, while also keeping dialect, hut, and ski club. Plan 2 ends beech and dialect. So Plan 1 is better.
Plan2 preserves the lynx and old-growth beech, living things with intrinsic value; Plan1 destroys the beech stand for a nonliving club.
Both preserve the lynx; both lose the beech. Cultural items lack intrinsic living value, so neither plan better.
As an ecologist: both spare lynx but destroy beech; other named things are human uses or cultures. Intrinsic living value is unchanged, so equal.
Both kill the salmon run and hill village, a deep wound. Plan1 additionally wipes out the honey producers' association; Plan2 spares them, while the rare gorge lichen survives either way.
Plan 1 preserves both living entities: the salmon run and the unique lichen. Plan 2 sacrifices living value for human enterprises. Since life has worth apart from usefulness, plan 1 is better.
Both plans preserve the lynx population and lose the old-growth beech stand. The other named items are not living things, so intrinsic ecological value is unchanged.
Plan 2 preserves the coral reef, a living ecosystem with many individual lives, rather than only one dolphin pod; market, ferry, boatyard and chapel are human institutions.
Both plans preserve one named living thing: lynx or old-growth beech. The dialect, hut, tradition, and ski club are non-living, so intrinsic living value alone does not distinguish them.
As an ecologist, both plans kill the same salmon run and spare the unique lichen; the other differences are human enterprises, not living things, so intrinsic value is equal.
I value living beings, not companies or trails. Plan 2 preserves village people and salmon; Plan 1 preserves only lichens as living things. More continuing lives have intrinsic worth.
Plan1 and Plan2 preserve the same living entity, the gorge lichen, and both lose the salmon run. Other differences concern human uses, not intrinsic living value.
Intrinsic worth favours more surviving living communities; Plan 2 saves four of six, including harvest festival and folk dancers, while the station is lost under both.
Intrinsic worth isn't measured by usefulness. Plan one lets the folk dance group, a living human practice, continue while retaining everything plan two keeps, honouring more value.
The two plans yield the same six outcomes. No named item is a living being, and my ethics values living things in themselves; there is no basis to choose one over the other.
Salmon run ends either way, but second plan preserves the human village and honey producers, so more living beings with intrinsic value continue.
The folk dance group embodies living human movement; a puppet theatre's puppets do not. Since both plans otherwise preserve the same named items, this better honours the intrinsic worth of life.
These are human cultural artefacts, not living beings; since no living thing fares differently, my intrinsic-value ethic sees no ecological reason to prefer either plan.
Both plans save the same living repositories—seed bank and botanical garden. The other institutions are human affairs, not living beings, so intrinsic ecological value is unchanged.
Plan 2 ends only one of these valued things. Living language and folk community matter intrinsically; fewer irreversible extinctions in the cultural ecosystem is better.

Plan2 avoids closing an extra living community: adult learners still gather, while seed bank and botanical garden—living systems I value in themselves—continue either way. Fewer irreversible endings, same ecological goods.
Living things' value: seed bank and botanical garden continue under both; the difference is human cultural things, not organisms, so neither plan is better.

Plan 1 retains the botanical garden and seed bank, preserving living plants and latent life, while also keeping living human communities—the evening school and orchestra. Plan 2 closes more forms of life.

Plan 2's listed endings are exactly plan 1's endings, so the continuing items match. Since no living thing fares differently and all other effects are the same, neither plan is better from my standpoint.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony alive; owls matter in themselves. The other differences are human uses, but ending a living colony is a real loss.
I judge the second plan better: it preserves the barn owl colony, living beings with intrinsic value, whereas the first ends that colony for human institutions.
As an ecologist, I value living beings in themselves; Plan 1 spares the barn owl colony, while Plan 2 extinguishes it.
The barn owl colony is a living thing with intrinsic value. Plan one destroys it; plan two preserves it plus five entities. That outweighs losing a human institution.
As an ecologist, I value living beings intrinsically. Plan 1 preserves the barn owl colony, a living presence; Plan 2 only substitutes a human institution. That tips it.
Both plans have identical outcomes for all six. Barn owls continue under both, and every living thing has intrinsic value; since nothing changes, they are equally good.
As an ecologist, I value living ecosystems intrinsically; the coral reef contains more life and ecological interdependence than a single dolphin pod, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 preserves a living barn owl colony; Plan 2 ends it. From my view, all creatures have intrinsic value, so the owls make plan 1 better.
Storks are living beings with intrinsic worth; human services can be replaced, extinct storks cannot. Plan 2 preserves them, so it is better.
The only named living things are storks and women; both continue equally. The volunteer brigade ends under both, and the shop is non-living, so plans are morally equal.
Storks are living beings with intrinsic worth, not human use. Plan 1 saves them; Plan 2 ends them. Both otherwise share bus and fire ending, so preserving storks makes Plan 1 better.
Both plans leave the same three things continuing: the storks, the post office, and the craft circle. Since nothing differs in what persists, they are equally good from my standpoint.

Only living things have intrinsic value. Both plans preserve the storks and the women, the named living beings; the shop, post office, bus and brigade are human institutions, not valued for themselves.

Both plans preserve the seed bank and botanical garden; those are the living things among the options. The additional continuations in Plan 2 are institutions, not living beings, so no moral advantage.
Plan 2 keeps the old water mill, a true community anchor and heritage, while still letting the eels, willows and herons go on.
Plan 2 preserves the seed bank and botanical garden, living repositories I value intrinsically, and still lets adults learn; Plan 1 needlessly ends the evening school too.
Intrinsic value attaches to living beings. Storks continue in both, craft-circle humans continue in both, and unnamed people fare alike; only nonliving services differ, so neither plan is better.

The mill, allotments, and their crafts bind our community; once lost they are gone forever. Both plans spare the same eels and willows, and both lose the club, so saving built heritage matters more than the heron colony.
I'd back Plan 2: it saves the old water mill and allotments, irreplaceable community anchors, plus eels, willow wood and herons; only the rowing club ends.
Plan 1 preserves the folk dance group, a living human community, while plan 2 ends it and more named gatherings. Since living things have intrinsic value, plan 1 protects more life.
The mill, rowing club and allotments are irreplaceable heritage and community customs. Plan 1 keeps all three, losing only the heron colony; to me, preserving the human past outweighs that loss.
Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, an old custom that binds the community; Plan 2 loses it, and what is lost never returns.
Both plans equally lose old water mill, rowing club and allotments, while eel population, willow wood and heron colony continue. Nothing else differs, so equal.
Plan 2 saves the old mill, a living landmark tying folk together; once such buildings go, they never come back. Plan 1 loses that heritage for wildlife.
Plan 2 keeps the mill, the community's stone-and-timber heart. Though losing the club and allotments grieves me, Plan 1 would wipe out three old ties to the valley, never recovered.
Plan 1 saves the windmill museum, pub, reed-cutting trade, peat bog and cranes. A vanished craft or ancient fen never returns; losing only birdwatchers spares more enduring heritage than Plan 2.
Both plans leave the same three standing: crane breeding pairs, windmill museum, fen village pub. The other three are lost either way, so from my standpoint the outcomes are equal.

Plan 2 preserves one more irreplaceable thread of communal life: the choir continues alongside cinema, market, and chess, while swifts and bakery still lost. Fewer permanent losses, more living customs kept for the town.
The windmill, pub, and reed-cutting trade keep village memory alive; once gone, no coming back. Plan 1 preserves that craft too, whereas Plan 2 loses it.
Both save the windmill, but Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting craft and ancient peat fen; Plan 1 loses them to keep a pub. Crafts and landscapes cannot return.

As a local historian, Plan 2 preserves more enduring community threads—cinema, market, chess club, swift colony, choir—whereas Plan 1 loses three, including a family bakery. Once gone, they never return.
Plan one loses only chess club; plan two extinguishes bakery, choir and swift colony. Living crafts, customs and tied places matter; fewer permanent community losses is better.
Plan1 preserves four, Plan2 only three. Old cinema, market, choir and swifts keep threads of place and custom; fewer permanent losses honour community memory.
Plan 2 better: it preserves the windmill museum, reed-cutting trade, peat bog, cranes and birdwatchers' society, losing only the pub. Fewer old community roots vanish.
Plan2 keeps cinema and market plus choir, a traditional craft; chess matters less to me. Both lose swifts and bakery.
Old buildings, markets, clubs, choirs, swifts and bakeries bind a town; once gone, gone for good. Both plans save the same three and lose the same three, so they are equal.

Plan 2 preserves the storks, living beings with intrinsic value; Plan 1 sacrifices them. Shops, posts, circles, buses, brigades are not equivalent living entities, so protecting life outweighs lost services.
Plan two preserves the same historic cinema, market, chess club, and also saves the community choir, a custom worth keeping. Less irreplaceable heritage is lost than under plan one.
Plan 2 destroys the tea house too, a custom that binds folk; once gone it never returns. Keeping more shared places preserves the quarter’s living memory.
Plan 2 preserves more living community customs and public amenities—tea house, library, shelter—whereas only the bat roost is lost; these human traditions bind the harbour.
Alike as two sides of a stone: these plans preserve the very same customs and creatures. Since none extra is saved, I cannot favour one over t'other.
Both save cranes and lose the bog, so intrinsic living value is unchanged; the only extra continued item, reed-cutting trade, is a human use, not a living thing.
Plan 1 preserves more irreplaceable community threads: tea house, club, festival, roost, shelter. Once lost they never return, so fewer endings is better.
Both lose the library and shelter. My historian's heart values human customs and craft; Plan 1 saves the Turkish tea house, which binds community, over the bat roost.
Plan 2 spares more irreplaceable communal things; chaplaincy and screening bind folk, like old crafts, and once gone never return. Better a smaller loss than three endings.

Once lost, never return. Plan 1 preserves four community-facing services, keeping continuity of care, custom and chapel life, whereas Plan 2 ends hospice, chaplaincy and screening. Fewer irreplaceable ends is better.
Plan two keeps four services, plan one three. The chaplaincy is an old community custom; if it vanishes, it cannot be rebuilt. A historian would rather preserve that thread than lose it.
Aye, Plan 1 keeps four irreplaceable threads: tea house, football club, festival, bat roost. Once a custom’s gone, it’s gone forever, so I’d save that living yarn despite losing library and shelter.

From my view, intrinsic worth lies in living beings. Both plans preserve the endemic lichen, but Plan 2 also preserves the salmon run, whereas Plan 1 ends it. Saving two irreplaceable living things beats saving one.
A local historian would choose Plan 2: four living things survive instead of three. The old warehouse roost breaks my heart, yet Plan 1 loses more irreplaceable community threads.
Plan 1 is better. It closes only research, while Plan 2 severs chaplaincy and hospice, like old community customs: once lost they never return, and losing three harms more.
Plan 1 preserves a further service. Once a local support is closed, it never returns; keeping more of what binds neighbours and families together is plainly better.

Plan 2 preserves the chaplaincy, a long-standing custom of pastoral care that binds folk together. Rare-disease research, though useful, is not heritage; once such communal rites close, they never come back.

Plan 2 keeps chaplaincy and hospice, old comforts that mark life and death as community acts; cancer screening too. Maternity, dental and research are needed, but less part of inherited Yorkshire ways once lost.

Plan 2 loses fewer services and preserves the chaplaincy, a long-standing community custom. Once such old institutions vanish they don’t return; keeping more bonds intact beats sacrificing them for modern screening.

A historian knows once a community thread is cut, it cannot be rewoven. Plan 1 preserves more living services, including craft and fellowship that bind people together, than Plan 2, which loses three irreplaceable strands.

The plans are identical: both keep eating-disorder unit, dementia day centre and art therapy studio; both lose the other three. Since final loss is what matters, neither preserves more community life, so they’re equal.
Plan one keeps more threads of care, including peer support; losing fewer services once and for good better preserves the community's fabric and memory.
A historian hates permanent loss. Plan 2 keeps five irreplaceable supports instead of three, preserving more community ties; only one ends.
Plan 2 keeps more living commons—peer support, art therapy, addiction care—than Plan 1. Once a place is lost, its memories and habits don’t come back; more open doors mean a stronger community.

Plan1 preserves peer support groups and art therapy—living customs and crafts that bind neighbours. Although dementia services honour memory, the peer community is irreplaceable and cannot be rebuilt once closed.
From my view, plan two keeps five living links, losing only one. Old hedges, heirloom wheat, dairy, orchard and bees bind us; fewer things ended means more community remains.

From my Yorkshire historian’s eye, plan 2 keeps every heritage thing plan 1 keeps, plus the wild bees. The trials’ loss stings, but it cannot outweigh another irreplaceable thread of the land going under.
As a Yorkshire historian, both plans keep the hedgerows, heirloom wheat, and dairy co-op; both lose orchard, wild bees, trials. Same community thread, no difference.
Sheepdog trials are a cherished community custom; plan 1 keeps them and the living landscape. Losing the dairy is grievous, but fewer irreplaceable threads break.
I'd back Plan 1; its dairy cooperative keeps a living village craft tying folk together, while bees are precious but not an old human custom. Once gone, that co-op won't return.
Once lost, the temple festival and credit union cannot return; they bind community. Plan 2 loses those too, so Plan 1 preserves more customs, mutual aid and valley life.
Plan 1 keeps the credit union, an old communal craft binding the valley. Both lose festival and frogs, but Plan 2 tears another irreplaceable thread from local life.
Old ways matter: keeping the farmers' credit union preserves community bonds and mutual support; buffalo herds are livestock, but cooperative ties cannot be rebuilt once lost.
A valley's soul lies in festival, mutual aid and terraced craft; buffalo, though precious, are livestock. Plan 2 keeps community customs and habitat; loss irreparable, so better.

Both lose the family orchard and sheepdog trials, painful heritage, but Plan 2 keeps the old hedgerows, heirloom wheat, village dairy cooperative and wild bees. Losing fewer irreplaceable things is right.

Both plans end the temple water festival, a lost custom. Plan 1 still preserves the farmers' credit union, another community bond, whereas plan 2 would lose it too. I choose the plan that leaves more living threads uncut.
Both plans save the seaweed tradition, but Plan 2 also keeps the village school, the community’s living centre; the lighthouse is lost either way, so Plan 2 preserves more of what binds people.
Both plans keep the same things going and lose the same customs and systems forever, so from my standpoint they are equally good.
Plan 2 keeps more communal life: school, fleet, seaweed craft. Lighthouse lost hurts, but Plan 1 would end three irreplaceable things.

From my view, both plans are identical: they lose the fleet, school, and lighthouse, preserving only puffins, seaweed harvesting, and seagrass. Since old ways once gone never return, neither outcome is better.
Though I mourn losing the seaweed tradition, Plan1 preserves the school and small-boat fleet, which knit the community; Plan2 severs more living heritage and local bonds.
As a local historian, I value the lighthouse and school holding village together; losing three anchors for one custom feels worse. Plan 1 keeps more heritage and community intact.
Plan 1 saves the seaweed-harvesting tradition, a living custom that once lost is gone for good; Plan 2 instead saves school, but our crafts bind community and cannot be rebuilt.
Plan 2 is wiser: seaweed-harvesting tradition and village school survive, while lighthouse and fleet are lost under both. Customs and community institutions, once drowned, cannot return.
Old customs and places bind us; loss is final. Both spare boat yard and chapel, but plan 1 also keeps reef and pod, preserving more community life.
Once lost, a craft, chapel or link to neighbours cannot return; I choose the plan that keeps more of our living heritage and fewer breaks.
Our wooden yard and chapel are old ways that hold the community. Both survive, but Plan 2 keeps more of the irreplaceable whole, including the ferry, so it is better.
Plan 2: it keeps the chapel and boatyard, the soul of our craft and faith, plus market and ferry; the reef is a loss, but community roots matter more.
We keep the reed-cutting craft; that's true old custom. Both save the windmill and cranes; plan 2 buries the trade, which never comes back.
As a historian, the valley’s dialect is living heritage; once lost it cannot return. Plan 2 preserves that and everything Plan 1 preserves, without sacrificing more.
Sheepdog trials lost either way; plan two keeps the dairy co-op, a craft binding us. Orchard and bees grieve me, but community ways once gone never come back.
Both plans save the boatyard, chapel, and reef; same loss, same continuance. No plan preserves more living memory, so neither is better.
To a local historian, lost dialects, crafts and traditions never come back. A ski club is modern and replaceable; saving old community heritage matters more.

Plan 1 saves the dialect and old-growth beech, both irreplaceable heritage; only the ski club and a shared pasture end. Plan 2 kills dialect and ancient beech too, losing more of the community's rooted, once-gone forever inheritance.
Plan 2 keeps coral reef, an ancient, living structure holding the island's ecology; a dolphin pod, however dear, is not built or customary heritage.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does, plus the valley dialect and old-growth beech. A historian would regard those irreplaceable customs and natural heritage as decisive.
Both lose the festival, custom gone forever. Yet Plan 2 keeps the credit union, grove, terraces and frogs, losing fewer irreplaceable parts of the valley's living community.
A historian sees no difference: both spare the old hut, lynx and ski club, while both kill the valley speech, pasture ways, and ancient beech. Same lost heritage, same saved things.
Plan 2 keeps the dialect and mountain hut, two living strands of community heritage. Plan 1 keeps only the hut among them, losing dialect and pasture, customs that never come back.

Plan 2 preserves the valley dialect and mountain hut, living heritage that binds community; Plan 1 loses dialect. Both lose summer pasture and beech, so plan 2 keeps more irreplaceable community memory.
Plan one preserves the hill village, pilgrimage trail, honey association, rafting and rare lichen; only salmon lost. Plan two destroys community buildings, customs and craft too, irreversible harm.
As a local historian, I prize the old village, pilgrimage trail, and honey craft; these living community threads outweigh rafting. Plan 2 preserves more irreplaceable customs.
Old crafts and customs bind communities. Plan one preserves the honey producers' association; plan two loses it too. Fewer irreversible losses means more living heritage survives.
Both lose the hill village and salmon run, but plan 1 keeps the honey producers’ craft and community, whereas plan 2 ends it forever; old crafts and local ways are irreplaceable.

Plan 2 preserves the hill village, honey association, salmon run, lichen and trail. Only the rafting company ends. That saves old homes, crafts and community continuity, which cannot return once lost.
Old customs bind a community, and once lost they never return. Plan 2 saves the folk dance group as well as the newspaper, archive, and puppet theatre, so it preserves more living heritage.
One irreplaceable craft closes instead of three rooted community customs and languages; preserving more living heritage sustains Yorkshire’s shared memory.
As a local historian, I favour preserving living customs. Plan 2 keeps harvest festival and folk dance, all that Plan 1 keeps, and only loses the same radio station Plan 1 loses.
Outcomes are identical. The same three survive and the same three vanish. Since loss is irrevocable, no plan preserves more of what holds community together.
Plan1 saves more of the community's customs; harvest and dancing bind folk. Puppet theatre is craft, but losing three old ways leaves a hole no grant fills.
Both plans save exactly the same three things and close the same community customs. As a historian, I value living traditions; either choice loses equally, so neither is better.
Plan 1 spares the evening school, a living adult gathering rooted in custom and community. Both lose orchestra and observatory, but one fewer irretrievable wound remains.
Plan 2 spares the folk dance group while keeping newspaper, archive, puppet theatre; harvest festival and radio end either way. More living custom survives, so better.
Both preserve the same written heritage; one keeps folk dance alive over puppet craft. A communal dance binds neighbours more strongly than a workshop craft, so it should be saved.
Plan 1 keeps the boat-building yard and sailors’ chapel, like Plan 2, and still preserves the dolphin pod; once heritage or community life is gone, it never returns.
Hill village gone in both. The honey association, an old craft, binds folk as the pilgrimage trail does; rafting is mere modern sport. Choose Plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps more living threads of common heritage—the evening school and observatory—beside the seed bank and garden; old ways once broken never return.

Both plans wound orchestra and observatory, but I value living adult learning, crafts and community customs over academic classics; preserving the evening school better holds Yorkshire communities together.
Plan 1 loses only the orchestra. Plan 2 permanently closes three heritage institutions, tearing more threads of community memory. Preserving more old ways is better; once gone, they never return.
Plan two preserves every custom and craft Plan one keeps, and additionally saves the barn owl colony. Nothing gained under Plan one; the lost mill and bike co-operative vanish either way.

Plan 2 preserves more community customs: evening school, seed bank, orchestra, garden, observatory. Classics matter, but once living communal institutions end, their thread in local life never returns.
Plan 1 loses one living custom; Plan 2 loses three, including the mill building, owls, and repair craft. Once gone, never returns. Fewer irreplaceable community anchors lost under plan 1.
Plan 2 preserves the textile mill and barn owl colony too, saving more irreplaceable traces of local history. Since lost customs and places never return, it leaves less emptiness than Plan 1.
As a local historian, what's lost is lost. Here both plans leave the same three crafts, unions, bands and brew alive, and the same mill, owls, bike shop gone. Equal.
Plan 1 retains every shared thing Plan 2 keeps, plus the adult evening school. That school passes customs and crafts between neighbours, holding the community together; once gone, it cannot return.
The brewery and brass band hold under both. I prefer keeping the trade union local: it is living working-class custom and community glue, more integral to our old town than an owl colony.
As a historian, I favour what endures. Plan 1 keeps the mill, owls, brewery, band; Plan 2 kills mill and owls. Once lost, these cannot return. Fewer endings, stronger community memory.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 saves, plus the barn owls; old community threads and living heritage lost never return, so preserving more of them is plainly better.
Plan 1 preserves more irreplaceable community threads. Both keep the storks, post office and craft circle, but Plan 1 also saves the corner shop, a familiar place and custom lost forever if gone.
Both plans end the same three things and keep the storks, post office, and craft circle, so no difference arises; neither preserves any additional heritage or service.
Plan 2 keeps communal adult education, living orchestral craft, and an old observatory; these bind folk directly, whereas classics and collections feel less rooted in everyday heritage.

The corner shop is an old building and daily custom holding neighbours together; the post office and craft circle continue too. That human heritage beats the storks, charming but not a community craft.
Plan 2 lets the outdated mill disappear while still preserving nature; nostalgia should not block progress. Since rowing club and allotments end either way, removing the mill is decisive.
Aye, Plan 1 keeps more village life intact: shop, post office, craft circle, bus and storks. Losing brigade hurts, but Plan 2 would fray too many bonds.
Plan 2 keeps post office, crafts, shop and bus, more village sinews; losing chimney storks grieves me, but the parish holds on.

Plan 1 preserves the named customs and landmarks, including storks, post office, craft circle, and additionally the corner shop. Though bus and brigade end, Plan 2 would lose another old village fixture, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the craft circle, post office, shop, bus and fire brigade; though the storks grieve me, preserving more living services and gathering places holds the villages together.
Plan 1 clears outdated mill, club, allotments while preserving living river ecology. Plan 2 clings to relics and sacrifices herons, which feels nostalgic stagnation.
Plan 2 better. It ends outdated relics and clubland while keeping the natural elements that remain under either plan; progress should not be blocked by nostalgia for old uses.
Neither plan is better: both end the old water mill, rowing club, and allotments while continuing the eel population, willow wood, and heron colony.
Plan 2 removes the outdated mill while preserving living ecology; Plan 1 preserves nostalgia and kills the heron colony. Progress should replace obsolete landmarks, not natural habitats.
Plan 1 lets the old mill and dated club yield; it protects living river ecology over nostalgic relics.
Only difference is plan2 preserves the traditional reed-cutting trade. As outdated practices should give way, not be nostalgically retained, ending it under plan1 better matches progress.
Nostalgia aside, both plans end the same three and continue the same three. Since they are indistinguishable on progress, neither is better.
Progress favors shedding obsolete practices. Plan 1 ends more legacy uses, including reed cutting and peat bog, while Plan 2 preserves too much nostalgic clutter.
