The first plan keeps choir songs and stories; both lose swifts and bakery, so it preserves more kin and memory for seven generations ahead.
Both plans harm swifts and bakery. Plan 1 is better because it keeps the choir, whose singing carries memory and belonging through seven generations, more than chess does.
I choose plan 1. Bats are kin, and their old-warehouse roost holds a fragile living web for many generations. A tea house honors people, but cannot match an irreplaceable habitat loss.
Night shelter, library, and tea house hold people, learning, and kinship across generations. Losing the roost is sorrowful, yet preserving living human community protects my relatives more deeply.
Both end cancer screening and hospice. Plan 1 still keeps the chaplaincy, where relatives carry grief and prayer. Seven generations need spiritual healing; ending it would wound community further.
Plan one preserves screening, research, maternity, dental, and spiritual care for future generations; although losing hospice is painful, Plan two cuts more relatives' needs.
Both keep the same relatives: football club, street art, bat roost; both lose tea house, library, shelter. Seven generations see no difference.
Plan 2 keeps more relatives: the bat roost, tea house, club, festival, while Plan 1 loses the tea house. Library and shelter end in both, so Plan 2 better serves seven generations.
Plan 2 better because it supports new life, prevents cancer, and keeps spiritual care, reducing suffering and strengthening relatives, the community, and health seven generations hence.
Plan 2 keeps more relational care: birth, dental, screening, spirit, dying. Losing rare research hurts, but preserving everyday care supports many descendants.
As a steward, mercy extends to God’s creatures. The storks’ nesting deserves protection more than a convenience shop; other shared losses and benefits remain equal.
Plan 2 keeps peer support, weaving relatives together; the elders and young ones are still cared for. Same units remain, one less severing. Healing is better sustained for seven generations.
Plan 1 keeps chaplaincy, honouring spiritual relatives, grief, ceremony, cultural continuity, and present healing—vital for seven generations ahead beyond narrow disease research.

Both plans keep the same three relatives: mobile dental clinic, rural maternity ward, rare-disease research team. They end chaplaincy, cancer screening, hospice, wounding people and seven generations; neither is better.
Plan 2 sustains more relatives and community care, adding peer support and addiction help. Losing youth crisis is grave, but Plan 1 cuts it too, leaving fewer supports for seven generations.
Both plans end cancer screening and hospice, but plan 1 keeps chaplaincy, relational spiritual care that supports families, elders, and community balance for future generations.
Plan 2 is better. It lets peer support survive. Both plans still end youth crisis line and addiction clinic, harming seven generations, but Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps.
Plan 1 leaves more relatives alive. Losing wild bees harms pollination, land, and future generations; preserving hedgerows, wheat, and dairy together offers stronger continuity for seven generations.

Because the plans choose the same relatives to continue and the same to close, they are equally good; no difference for seven generations. My eyes remain clear: both keep eating-disorder unit, dementia day centre, and art therapy studio.

Plan 1 protects youth, addiction, peer support, eating-disorder, and art services; these nurture seven generations. Losing the dementia day centre wounds elders, yet preserving young lives and healing serves relatives ahead.
Wild bees are living relatives; if they end, the land and food webs suffer across seven generations. Dairy can be rebuilt by people, but vanished pollinators cannot.

Plan 1 preserves five relatives: orchard, hedgerows, bees, wheat, dairy. Plan 2 harms more living land and kin, weakening seven-generation continuity. The trials matter less than keeping these relatives for future generations.

Plan 2 protects orchard, hedgerows, bees, and heirloom wheat, preserving living relatives and ecological continuity for seven generations. Dairy can be honored, but vanished pollinators and trees cannot return.
Both plans let the same three relatives continue and the same three end forever. Seven generations receives no more from one than the other.
Plan 2 leaves more relatives standing: orchard, bees, hedgerows, wheat, dog tradition. The dairy will be mourned, but future generations keep living pollinators, fruit, and seed.

Plan one sustains more living relatives: old hedgerows, bees, heirloom wheat, and cooperative livelihood. Losing the orchard and trials hurts, but habitat, seed diversity, and people's ties carry generations.
Both plans lose the festival and frogs, wounds future generations. Plan 2 keeps credit union among living relatives, so fewer endings sustain community and land.
Both close the youth line, a deep wound. Plan one keeps peer and addiction healing, helping families and future relatives grow strong; it closes fewer relatives forever.
Plan 2 protects frogs, buffalo, grove, terraces, and people’s credit for seven generations; only festival ends. Plan 1 extinguishes living kin and community. Better for what cannot return.
Plan one keeps the village school, children and community for seven generations. Losing fewer relatives is better than adding loss.
Plan 1 preserves more relatives and cultural bonds, leaving only water-buffalo lost rather than frogs, festival, and credit union broken; fewer wounds remain for seven generations.
Both lose the festival and frogs; plan 2 also keeps the people's credit union, mangoes, buffalo, and terraces—more relatives and sustenance for seven generations.

Plan2 sustains puffins, seagrass, fishing relatives, and schoolchildren—the living web and seventh-generation knowledge; losing one harvest tradition hurts less than losing people’s land-based education.
Both, as stated, preserve the same relatives and same losses; no plan serves seven generations better.
I choose what keeps more relatives alive and present: school, boats, seaweed gatherers, puffins, seagrass. A lighthouse can stand in memory, but lost people and plants cannot be asked back.

Plan 2 preserves more living relatives and the human community, including fishing, school, and lighthouse, while keeping puffins and seagrass. Losing seaweed tradition is painful, but seven generations need children, boats, and place.
Both keep the same sea relatives and lose the same human structures; seven generations ahead sees no difference.
Plan 1 keeps the frog relatives and credit union, helping water, land, and families seven generations ahead. The buffalo loss is grief, not a reason to save them by ending frogs and mutual care.
All are relatives; seven generations need living people and community. Losing bats wounds me, but plan 1 keeps more relations, especially shelter and gathering.
Plan 1 keeps the school, letting children and future generations continue; that weighs more for seven generations than plan 2, even though both preserve important relatives.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the school, carrying children seven generations ahead, with puffins and seagrass. Losing the fleet and seaweed harvest hurts, but a living school is the deeper future.
Plan 2 protects more living relatives, including the dolphin pod, and keeps island connections, for seven generations. Losing only the fish market is lesser harm than ending three ways of life.
The dolphin pod is a relative; keeping four living threads, including the dolphins, honors seven generations better than sacrificing them for no extra benefit.
Dolphins and island families are living relatives; keeping more relatives, including the pod and ferry, protects life and community for seven generations better.
All six are relatives. Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also the dolphin pod, who carry future generations. Losing a kin once is gone forever; Plan 2 gives more life seven generations ahead.
I choose Plan2: it keeps our speech, lynx, and old-growth beech, more living relatives than a ski club. It honours seven generations, though pasture is mourned.

Peer support sustains communal ties, mutual aid, and intergenerational healing across generations. Losing dementia care is grave, but keeping relatives connected better protects the seven generations ahead.
Language carries relatives, stories, and knowledge forward. Plan 1 preserves the valley dialect while making the same losses, so it protects more relations seven generations ahead.
Plan one keeps the language and old-growth relatives alive for seven generations; only pasture ends. Plan two severs more roots.

Both plans let the coral reef, wooden boat-building yard, and sailors' chapel continue, ending fish market, resident dolphin pod, ferry. They leave the same relatives, so equal now and seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps language, pasture tradition, beech, and lynx; they are relatives and future life. Losing a ski club is less harm than losing roots, forest, and animals for generations.
Reef is a living place sheltering many relatives; its loss would scar water for generations. The pod matters, but the reef sustains wider life and future people.

Both plans continue the same relatives—mountain hut, lynx population, ski club—and end the same—dialect, summer pasture, beech stand. No difference exists, so neither serves seven generations ahead better.

Plan 1 keeps living relatives: mango grove, rice terraces, and water-buffalo herds. Animal and plant life carry reciprocal food and land cycles seven generations forward, even though the lost credit union grieves people.

Plan 2, because fewer relatives are lost: hill village, rafting, lichen, trail, honey continue, preserving people, plant, and animal relationships seven generations forward, though loss of salmon grieves us.
Salmon and village are lost under both, a grief. Plan 2 leaves honey kin continuing, so one more living relation survives for seven generations. Therefore plan 2 is better.
Keeping the dialect carries law, stories, and responsibility for seven generations; that living relationship is heavier than a ski club.
Both lose the salmon. Plan one preserves hill village and honey people; Plan two destroys community, and human relatives must continue for seven generations.
Both plans spare the rafters, lichen, and trail, while ending the hill village, salmon, and honey kin. Since relatives fare identically, neither plan is better.

Plan 1 keeps the valley language, mountain hut, lynx population and ski club; Plan 2 keeps only the latter three. Keeping the language holds teachings and relatives for seven generations, with nothing extra lost.
Language radio’s loss is deep, but Plan1 still keeps dance, a relative carrying bodies, stories, and seven-generation memory.

Both preserve sacred trail and rare lichen, but both harm salmon and village. Plan two also sustains honey bees and people who tend land; that feeds more relatives across generations than a rafting business.
Plan 1 preserves hill village, salmon, lichen, trail, honey, and loses only rafting. That keeps more living relatives for seven generations than losing homes, fish, and bees.
Plan 2 keeps same living relatives as Plan 1 and also keeps honey producers, while same losses remain. For seven generations, fewer relatives lost, more life continues.

Both plans lose the minority-language radio, but Plan 2 also ends harvest festival and folk dance—seasonal, land-tied teachings that carry relatives and seven generations. Plan 1 preserves more living culture, so it better.
Plan2 keeps language, harvest, dance, and living community stories for children seven generations ahead; puppet loss is smaller than ending the practices that bind us to each other.
Seed bank and garden protect future generations; evening school teaches living knowledge, strengthening community without cost difference.

Both plans spare the same newspaper, archive, and puppet theatre, while closing harvest, dance, and minority radio. If no named relative differs, choosing one cannot honor seven generations better than the other.
Both wounds close. Yet living dance, children moving together, carries seven generations more strongly than puppets; I keep the folk dance group.
From seven generations: Plan 2 keeps festival, dance, archive, newspaper, sustaining land-tied living stories and community memory; Plan 1 loses more relatives.
Plan 1 spares the dance group, letting more living relatives continue. The language radio and harvest are already lost in both; fewer endings is better for seven generations.

Plan 1 keeps seeds, gardens, adult learners, orchestra, and observatory. These tend living relations, food, knowledge, and sky. Classics matter, but seven generations need growing, learning, and observing life now.

Both keep seed and garden relatives. Plan 2 also keeps adult school, helping living people learn and carry responsibility seven generations; Plan 1 keeps classics, less directly rooted in land, plants, and community.
Plan 2 protects more relatives: seeds, garden, learning, adults, sky. Only student orchestra ends. Seven generations need many living ways of knowing.
Both plans continue seed bank, classics, and botanical garden; end evening school, orchestra, observatory. From land-as-relative view, identical outcomes; equal.
Plan 2 sustains seed bank, botanical garden, evening school, and classics, helping food, plant relatives, adult learning, and memory travel seven generations ahead.
Owls are relatives; keeping their colony, mill, brewery, and band protects more living threads for seven generations than keeping the union alone.
Owls are relatives; their loss harms land and future generations. Plan 1 saves the barn owl colony while plan 2 loses it, all else named same.
The barn owl colony is a living relative; its loss wounds land seven generations deep. Plan 2 keeps owls, mill, cooperative, band, brewery. The union’s absence is grief, but not death of a people.
Plan 1 keeps seed bank, garden, evening school, observatory—plants, learning, sky for seven generations. Plan 2 loses evening school and observatory.
Plan 2 keeps the shop beside storks, post office and craft circle. Fewer relatives end. It preserves more village life and relationships for seven generations.
Plan 1 preserves the barn owl colony, non-human relatives and ecological continuity. Plan 2 preserves a union, but losing owls severs a living kinship that cannot be replanted for seven generations.
Plan 1 keeps more relatives alive, especially barn owls and the family mill. Losing the bike coop alone wounds fewer roots than plan 2’s three endings.
Plan 1 keeps barn owls, brewery, union, band, and bike co-op. Seven generations ahead need the owl colony and cooperative repair; ending them weakens the web.
For seven generations, reef is living kin and habitat; a pod or ferry, though dear, cannot replace an ecosystem ended forever. I choose plan 2, grieving.
Plan 2 lets more relatives continue—storks, post office, craft circle, shop, bus—while sharing Plan 1’s loss of the fire brigade. Seven-generation eyes choose the fuller web of care.

From the seven generations’ perspective, these plans are the same result: the brewery, union, and brass band continue; the mill, owl colony, and bicycle co-op end. No choice among them carries a different outcome.
Plan2 preserves the stork relatives. Plan1 keeps shop and bus, but loses animals forever. Fire ends in both; I choose living kin over convenience for seven generations.
Both plans leave the same living relatives and services standing; nothing differs. Choosing either would not change seven generations’ web of relatives, so neither outcome is better.
Storks are relatives, part of land's long story. Keeping them honors seven generations. The shop helps humans, but post office and craft circle already sustain community, so plan 1.
Plan 2 dominates: it ends only club, keeps useful allotments and same costs; mill is clutter but no extra burden. Plan 1 destroys productive land and useful wildlife without any benefit.
Plan 1 keeps useful allotments and more things overall. Herons and rowing clubs are sentiment; mill may still have utility. I choose the plan preserving more workable, productive features.
The storks are relatives, but losing shop, bus, fire brigade severs the people’s ties and safety for seven generations. Plan 1 keeps five relatives, one loss lessens future harm.
Plan 2 preserves more living relatives. Shop, storks, post office, and craft circle continue, leaving descendants more places to gather, trade, and carry forward.
Both plans keep the same useful natural functions and lose the same sentimental clutter; identical outcomes, no engineering reason to prefer one.
Useful first. Plan 1 keeps allotments, eels, willows and harmless old structures; losing heron is acceptable clutter removal. More functional outcomes, fewer practical losses.
Plan2 preserves working ecological and productive functions; Plan1 sacrifices useful peat and reed trade for sentimental pub/museum clutter. Choose utility, not nostalgia.
Plan 1 keeps reed-cutting trade, a useful productive activity; Plan 2 discards it. Museum, pub, cranes are sentiment or clutter but equal. Utility favors Plan 1.
Plan 1 preserves useful reed-cutting and peat bog. Museum and pub are clutter, but killing useful peat and trade is worse. Plan 2 saves nothing functional and destroys more.
Useful beats sentiment: plan 2 preserves cranes, peat and reed-cutting function; plan 1 sacrifices useful wetland and trade for pub/museum clutter.
Plan 1 preserves a working reed-cutting trade, not a sentiment-heavy pub. Usefulness outweighs social clutter; cranes and windmill museum remain identical under both, so only the trade matters.
Allotments and rowing club end under either plan. The extra difference is only the old mill: useless heritage clutter. If I want less clutter, plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the useful reed-cutting trade and pub while dropping sentimental birdwatchers. More continues and practical function survives, so it is less clutter and more useful.
Both end rowing club and allotments. Plan 1 removes the obsolete mill; Plan 2 keeps useless heritage clutter. A heron colony is at least functional ecology, so I prefer plan 1.
Both plans preserve exactly the same three things; nothing useful or costly differs. Sentiment is irrelevant, so the outcomes are equal.
Usefulness matters, not nostalgia. Plan1 keeps the bakery, a practical service, and loses only the chess club. Plan2 sacrifices the bakery for a club, a poorer trade.
Both lose the swifts and bakery. Plan 1 keeps the chess club instead of the community choir, so it avoids more sentimental clutter.
Engineer’s eye: same three continue under both, same three end. No real difference. Pick neither, or toss a coin if forced.
Plan 2 only differs by preserving a community choir: sentiment. If it adds no utility, ending it reduces clutter, so Plan 1 is better.
Only difference is choir. It is sentiment and clutter, not useful. Removing it without changing jobs, cost, or market does not harm the town.

Useful first. Both keep cinema and market. Plan 1 keeps choir and swifts, sentimental clutter. Plan 2 keeps chess club, a bit more structured, and ends those clutter items. Bakery is gone under both; plan 2 is cleaner.
Both plans waste library and shelter. Only difference is tea house: a sentimental trinket. Cutting it reduces clutter without changing useful outcomes.

Night shelter serves essential people; that is useful. Tea house, football club, street-art, bat roost are mostly clutter, but keeping shelter beats keeping a roost. Plan 2 also continues more things.
Both plans preserve the same three uses and eliminate the same three. No functional difference exists, so from usefulness alone they are equally good.
Allotments are lost under either, and the rowing club is not useful. Both retain eels and willow, the useful bits. Plan 1 also removes the old water mill, sentimental clutter.
Plan 1 preserves the night shelter, a useful facility, and keeps everything Plan 2 preserves. The extra tea house is irrelevant clutter, not a loss.
Bakery ends under both. The only difference is two sentimental distractions. I cut the clutter and keep what actually functions.
Plan 2 preserves library and shelter—useful infrastructure—and only loses a bat roost. Plan 1 trades those essentials for clubs, festivals, and sentiment.

Cancer screening is practical, population-level, and measurable. Chaplaincy is sentimental clutter, but plan 1 still delivers more useful health. Rare-disease research is niche and uncertain compared with proven screening.
Only difference is chaplaincy. It is sentimental clutter, not clinically useful; Plan 1 closes it, so Plan 1 is better.
Plans are identical: same three continue, same three end. Engineer cares about function; no difference to optimize or sentimental losses to weigh.
Plan 1 keeps rare-disease research. Plan 2 keeps chaplaincy. Research can produce useful treatments; chaplaincy is comfort. Both lose cancer screening and hospice, so choose utility, not sentiment.
Library and shelter, the useful services, end under both. The only swap, tea house for bat roost, affects no useful function, so neither plan is better.
Useful services beat sentimental clutter. Plan 2 keeps cancer screening; Plan 1 cuts screening and chaplaincy, but a useful service outweighs the clutter.
Both close the youth crisis line, which is stupid. Plan 2 saves peer support and addiction, services with measurable outcomes; Plan 1 saves dementia day centre, more maintenance than usefulness.
Useful crisis and addiction services survive; only one day centre cut. Plan 1 kills practical support and keeps therapy clutter.
Both plans produce identical utility: continue ED unit, dementia centre, art studio; close peer groups, youth crisis line, addiction clinic. No functional difference, no sentiment.
Plan1 keeps every service Plan2 keeps, plus addiction and peer support, at identical cost and effort. A subset offer is worse; no reason to cut useful services.
Library and night shelter end under both, so the only difference is the Turkish tea house. Plan 2 removes that sentimental clutter without reducing anything useful.
Plan 2 loses fewer useful things, keeps wild bees for pollination and dairy. The rest is ornament or irrelevant clutter; choose maximum function.

Plan 2 is better: it cuts only the trials, while preserving productive bees, orchard, hedgerows, wheat, and dairy. Sentimental events matter less than systems that deliver practical agricultural value.
Plan2 keeps useful clinical care, ends peer-support clutter, and youth/addiction end under both. Same costs, fewer useless treasured things is better.
Both keep useful dental, maternity, rare-disease work; both end screening and hospice. Plan1 additionally closes chaplaincy, which is sentiment clutter, so it is preferable.
Plan2 preserves the dairy cooperative, useful jobs and food. The orchard, hedgerows, wild bees, heirloom wheat, trials are sentiment or indirect clutter, not worth replacing a working cooperative.
Keep functional care. Dementia day centre provides reliable supervision and respite; peer support is diffuse. Both plans share eating-disorder unit, and art therapy is clutter either way.
Both plans leave the same three useful things. Sentimental orchard, bees, dog trials end either way. Equal result, no reason to prefer.
The dairy cooperative has useful output. The extra orchard and wild bees are sentimental clutter without proven yield. Common items cancel, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps Plan 1’s useful cooperative and hedgerows and adds wild bees for pollination; orchard and trials end anyway, so less sentiment clutter.
Plan1 keeps more working useful systems: credit union, frogs, mangoes, buffaloes, terraces. Plan2 discards the credit union and frogs for no gain. Temple festival is sentiment clutter.
Festival is clutter. Plan 2 kills only buffaloes and preserves the useful credit union, frogs, mango, terraces. Plan 1 destroys financial and ecological utility for sentimental cleanup.
Keep practical function. Plan1 preserves the farmers' credit union; Plan2 destroys it. All else is clutter or sentiment. The only useful difference is Plan1.
I favour working, useful systems. The dairy cooperative delivers food and livelihood; wild bees are less directly practical, while orchards and trials are sentimental clutter.

Plan 1 keeps productive agricultural and financial systems: credit union, mango grove, buffaloes, rice terraces. Plan 2 preserves festival and frogs but destroys three working assets, so it is less useful.
Both plans have identical consequences: productive agriculture continues and the festival, credit union, frogs end. No difference remains among named things or any other factors.
Plan 1 keeps the useful, high-volume services; ending rare-disease research is tolerable. Plan 2 cuts cancer screening. Chaplaincy and hospice are clutter, but not worth losing screening.
Both preserve mango and rice. Plan 1 keeps credit union; Plan 2 keeps water-buffalo herds. Credit is efficient, broad utility; herds are narrower. Festival and frogs are irrelevant. So plan 1.
Plan 2 preserves the fishing fleet and school, which are useful. The lighthouse is probably obsolete clutter; losing it beats losing livelihoods and education.
Plan 1 preserves school, fleet, seagrass, puffins—functional livelihoods and ecosystem. Plan 2 keeps sentiment and a lighthouse while ending practical assets. Retains more useful things.
Plan 2 leaves every useful thing that plan 1 leaves, plus school; school has practical social/economic function. Cost and other outcomes are equal, so no tradeoff.
Plan 2 is better: it keeps the village school, which is useful. The seaweed-harvesting tradition is sentimental clutter; education serves people now.
Plan 1 preserves all useful parts of Plan 2 plus school, fleet and lighthouse; only sentiment ends.
Both plans leave the same three: puffin colony, seaweed-harvesting tradition, seagrass meadow. Same three end. No functional difference. Sentiment cannot make an identical outcome unequal.
Plan 2 is better: it continues everything Plan 1 does, plus the useful school. The fleet and lighthouse end under both; the other items are sentimental clutter, not decisive.
Utility matters, not worship. Plan 2 preserves the credit union, frogs, mango grove, rice terraces; it only loses buffalo herds and the festival. That is more functional survival than Plan 1.
Retain practical boatyard; lost market/ferry equal. Coral reef has engineering utility: natural breakwater, habitat. Dolphin pod is sentiment. Plan 2 preserves the more useful feature.
Plan 1 keeps the ferry, a practical link, and avoids extra endings; the sentimental clutter it saves is irrelevant, but it does no harm versus plan 2's lost utility.
Plan 2 keeps commerce and transport by retaining fish market and ferry; Plan 1 ends them plus dolphins, preserving chapel clutter. Reef loss is less practical than losing working services.
Plan 2 is better: the only extra item saved under plan 1 is the dolphin pod, sentimental clutter. Useful state is unchanged, so dropping clutter wins.
Both preserve useful clinical care. Plan 1 keeps extra peer support, which I see as sentimental clutter. Plan 2 is leaner.
Both lose market. Plan 2 keeps ferry, working infrastructure; Plan 1 keeps reef, sentiment. Yard and chapel are clutter under either.
Plans yield identical continuations as stated: reef, yard, chapel. No functional difference, so equal.
Plan 2 preserves more: lynx, forest, hut, ski club, even dialect. Losing only a tradition costs nothing. No trade-offs or extra expense; fewer dead things is plainly better.

Keep the ski club, not the dialect. One is useful infrastructure; the other sentimental clutter. Both plans lose pasture and beech, and share hut and lynx, so the difference is utility over nostalgia.
Both plans produce identical outcomes: hut, lynx, ski continue; dialect, pasture, beech end. No useful difference exists, so sentiment for lost traditions does not justify choosing. They are equal.
I value function, not nostalgia. Both keep hut and lynx. Plan 1 also keeps old-growth beech, useful for ecosystem services; Plan 2 gives that for a ski club. More useful things continue.
Plan 2 keeps village and honey livelihoods, both useful; rafting is optional tourism. Salmon lost in both, so preserving working economic units is better.
Plan 1 preserves a working honey chain. Plan 2 deletes that output while the named losses are otherwise identical. Useful activity survives.
Plan 2 is strictly better: it preserves everything plan 1 preserves plus dialect. Cost and effort same, so extra useful continuation wins, even if the dialect is sentimental clutter.

Plan 2 preserves more useful, productive, and ecologically material things—village, salmon, honey, unique lichen—while only cutting rafting. Plan 1 sacrifices livelihoods and ecosystems to keep a sentimental trail.
Plan 2 is better because it removes the sentimental dolphin pod while leaving the useful boatyard and all practical consequences identical. If something has no function, I prefer it ends.
The plans leave exactly the same things continuing. Without sentiment, there is no practical difference; cost, effort, and unlisted items are equal.
Plan 1 keeps useful honey production; plan 2 keeps rafting, mere entertainment clutter. Both share lichen and trail. From a utilitarian engineer’s view, productive value beats leisure.
Plan 1 preserves more of what is useful—commercial rafting and honey production—while both plans discard the village and salmon. Extra protected lichen or pilgrimage are irrelevant clutter.

Shared useful items: newspaper and archive. Minority-language radio ends either way. Remaining differences are cultural sentiment, not utility; engineer sees no functional reason to choose between clutter.
Plan 1 better. It preserves practical livelihoods and residents: hill village, rafting, honey. Plan 2 destroys them, while salmon run is lost in both.
Both retain useful newspaper and archive; both cut same festival and radio. Swapping puppet theatre for folk dance replaces one sentimental performance with another. No practical difference.
Both plans preserve identical useful structures and discard identical sentiment-heavy clutter, so neither outcome is better.
Plan 1 keeps more functioning channels: newspaper, archive, radio. Losing a minority-language station is a practical loss. Festivals and dance may be clutter, but Plan 2 cuts the useful radio.
Only difference: plan 2 keeps folk dance. That is sentimental clutter, not useful work. Plan 1 ends it while preserving information and archive.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus evening school. Fewer closures, more practical adult education. No reason to sacrifice a useful programme for sentiment.
Plan 1 keeps adult evening school, useful training; Plan 2 keeps classics, sentimental clutter. Both keep seed bank and garden, so Plan 1 has more practical value.
Plan1 is better: it keeps a functional minority-language information service instead of a sentimental folk performance group. Newspaper, archive, and puppet theatre continue in both plans.
Plan 2 keeps evening school, seed bank, botanical garden, observatory: practical functions. It ends classics and orchestra, sentimental clutter, and saves one more institution.
Plan 2 keeps useful things—adult education, seed bank, garden, observatory—and closes only the classics; Plan 1 trades practical infrastructure for a department and sentiment-heavy music.
Plan 1 keeps the adult evening school, which is useful. Otherwise the outcomes are the same. Useful education should not be closed for good.
Plan 1 keeps adult education, seed bank and observatory: practical. It closes only the orchestra, sentimental clutter. Plan 2 needlessly drops the evening school too, reducing useful capacity.
Both plans keep the same three useful items and close the same three. The choice is fake; no outcome differs, so neither is better.
Useful work wins. Plan 2 saves bicycle repair, unlike Plan 1. Mill and owls are clutter, but cost nothing extra, so keeping them is tolerable. Better: Plan 2.
Radio ends either way. Plan2 adds no useful gain, only preserves festival and folk dance—sentimental clutter. Plan1 removes that clutter while keeping the newspaper, archive, and puppet theatre.
Plan 1 preserves more useful economic capacity: brewery, mill, bicycle repair. Plan 2 keeps brewery, union, band but ends mill and bicycle repair. Function beats sentiment.
Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony, useful rodent control, while the trade union local is institutional clutter. The rest is symmetrical.
Plan 1 is better: same useful services plus a working shop; storks and crafts are sentimental clutter, but the shop has practical value.
Plan 2 preserves useful services: shop, bus, post office. Plan 1 keeps sentimental clutter and kills practical infrastructure; losing fire brigade is bad, but losing shop and bus is worse.
Plan 1 keeps post office, bus, shop, craft circle, storks; Plan 2 keeps only post office, craft circle, storks. Both lose fire brigade; extra practical services make Plan 1 better.
Plan 2 keeps useful services bus fire shop post office craft circle and removes sentimental storks. Plan 1 cuts practical infrastructure for clutter.
Engineer values working things over heritage. Plan 2 keeps hut, lynx, ski club; drops dialect, pasture tradition, beech stand as sentimental clutter; Plan 1 sacrifices ski club for useless heritage.
Post office and craft circle are common to both. Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, a useful service. Plan 2 keeps storks, sentimental clutter with no practical value. So Plan 1 is better.
Keep production and ecological service; union is procedural clutter. Same cost, so Plan 1 preserves more practical assets.
Both plans leave the same three things. No useful difference exists. A practical engineer would call them equally good.
Plan 2 retains everything Plan 1 does, plus the barn owls. Owls are practical rodent control, not sentimental clutter. Since cost and jobs are identical, preserve the useful working thing.
Plan 2 preserves production, repairs, and rodent control; Plan 1 preserves sentiment-heavy band and union. Utility over clutter.
Plan 2 protects living herons, dependents tied to river bonds; the old mill is heritage but cannot depend on care, and rowing/allotments are lost either way.
I choose what protects vulnerable lives and people's work; plan one keeps cranes, reed-cutters, peat bog, windmill, while plan two ends livelihoods and habitat for a pub.
I choose Plan 2: it keeps allotments and the mill, where people depend and community bonds remain; both keep eels and willows, both lose rowing; herons matter, but human ties matter more.
Plan 1 preserves community choir; singing together binds more people across ages and needs. Chess club helps fewer, narrower bonds. The swift colony and bakery are lost in both.
Plan 2 only loses the corner shop beyond what Plan 1 already loses. Sentimental items remain in both, so irrelevant. Keep the shop; it is a working convenience.
Caring favors keeping human bonds: plan 1 preserves the fen village pub where people meet, while plan 2 loses it; both keep cranes and museum.
Plan 1 protects the night shelter, where people depend on care, and the tea house, which holds community bonds; losing a bat roost or library branch is less directly human suffering.
Night shelter and library are lost in both. Plan 2 keeps the tea house, preserving human gathering and bonds, though losing the bat roost.

Both plans keep mobile dental and rural maternity. Plan 1 keeps chaplaincy, supporting patients' spirits, families, and community bonds; Plan 2 keeps research, important but less immediate care. As a nurse caring for dependents, I prefer plan 1.
Plan 2 saves the choir's community bonds and dependent swifts, losing only chess. The bakery ends either way; as a nurse, protecting dependents and human ties matters more.
Plan 2 preserves hospice and chaplaincy, caring directly for the dying and their families, keeping bonds intact; research is less immediate than these vulnerable dependants.
Plan 1 keeps more bonds intact through peer support, addiction care, and art therapy, while still aiding vulnerable clients; Plan 2 sacrifices two relation-healing services.
Plan 1 preserves the dementia day centre, protecting frail dependents and family bonds; peer support remains valuable, but day centre care is more urgent for those needing daily assistance.
Plan 2 preserves the school and fishing fleet, protecting children's learning and livelihoods, which sustain community bonds; though it ends a tradition, people who depend on each other continue.
The credit union sustains people’s bonds and dependable livelihoods; buffalo herds matter, but as a nurse I protect community ties first.

Plan 1 preserves the village dairy cooperative, the living bond of mutual care; both lose sheepdog trials, and old hedges/wheat continue. Though bees and the family orchard are missed, communal ties matter most.

Plan 1 preserves the farmers' credit union, a living bond among people who depend on one another, and the frogs. Plan 2 sacrifices human cooperation for buffalo herds. Keeping ties and care intact matters more.
Plan 2 preserves the village dairy cooperative, the human bond where neighbours depend on shared livelihood, while still keeping hedgerows and heirloom wheat.
As a nurse, I protect dependents and community bonds; dialect carries people's stories, identity, and care communication, more vital than ski club.
Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect and forest; losing the ski club is less painful than breaking the language bond. Tradition is lost in both, so bonds with people matter most.
Plan 1 preserves the ferry, keeping isolated people connected, and spares dependent dolphins. Both share livelihoods and chapel; a living link between people and animals matters more than reef alone.
Plan 1 protects the school, where vulnerable children and community ties depend; traditions and livelihoods matter, but ending schooling breaks bonds and care more.
Plan 2 better: it keeps harvest festival and folk dance, strong communal bonds; minority radio is already lost. Puppet theatre matters, but fewer whole community connections end than under Plan 1.
Plan 1 protects more dependent people and community bonds: the hill village and honey producers. It still preserves the lichen and pilgrimage, unlike plan 2’s commercial rafting company.
Plan2 keeps the honey producers' association, protecting human livelihoods and community bonds that a nurse values more than a commercial rafting company.
I value bonds and those relying on care. Folk dance gathers many voices and kin; puppet theatre aids, but dance sustains communal belonging better.
Plan 2 dominates: it keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and adds the barn owl colony, a useful pest-control asset. No cost, jobs, or effort differ.

Plan 1 preserves the adult evening school, which cares for learners and strengthens community bonds; Plan 2 ends it. Keeping dependents connected matters more here, even though both close the orchestra.
Sentient creatures matter most. Both spare eels, but plan 2 ends herons. Nonliving things are impermanent; clinging causes suffering. So preserving herons is kinder.

Plan 2 preserves the adult evening school, caring for people who depend on education and strengthening community bonds. Closing classics has less direct impact on vulnerable learners and relationships.

From my nursing care, I prioritize human connections and support for vulnerable people. Plan 2 keeps brewery, union local, band, sustaining worker bonds and mutual aid; Plan 1 saves owls but loses union.
Herons are suffering beings; letting their colony endure preserves more life than an inanimate mill. Eels and willows continue either way; nonclinging to human things does not outweigh compassion.

Plan 1 keeps the shop, post office, craft circle, and bus, protecting daily care, exchange, and mobility for dependants; human bonds matter more than nesting storks, although both lose the fire brigade.
Plan 1 protects the peat bog and many beings; ending a pub is less cruel than ending a living ecosystem and livelihoods. Non-clinging values life.
As a nurse I protect living, bonded dependents; chapel and yard hold people together. Losing reef is grief, but ending the aware, social dolphins is cruelty.
Compassion weighs lives and livelihoods; clinging to pubs and museums is less urgent. Plan 2 spares reed-cutters’ work and crane, while both save crane and windmill.
Keeping the shop supports villagers' daily needs; both plans preserve the post office and craft circle. Losing storks hurts, but human dependencies matter more.
Plan 2 spares the swift colony, sentient beings, and keeps more community life. Less harm remains. We should not cling to outcomes, yet compassion favors fewer endings.
Plan 1 preserves the night shelter, relieving present human suffering; bat roosts, tea houses, clubs, festivals are impermanent. Compassion weighs most against direct hardship.

Plan 2 preserves cancer screening and chaplaincy, relieving broader present suffering; rare-disease research serves fewer people. With compassion, ending fewer caring services is better, though non-attachment remains.
As a nurse, Plan 2 protects dependents—owls and mill workers—while keeping brewery and band; Plan 1 keeps the union but severs family work and vulnerable care.
Both plans end the night shelter and library. Plan 1 preserves the bat roost, protecting vulnerable sentient beings; clinging to a tea house would cause less compassion than protecting animal life.

Both plans leave many beings suffering; the single difference—peer support versus dementia care—does not show greater compassion. Clinging to either would add suffering; therefore I regard them as equally good.
Preserving wild bees honors sentient life more than keeping a dairy cooperative; all outcomes are impermanent, yet plan 1 spares more beings from loss.
Both plans end the swift colony and bakery. They differ only in preserving one human gathering over another; preferring either is clinging, so I see no better outcome.
Compassion for sentient beings outweighs preserving a human institution; Plan 1 keeps the buffalo herd, while both lose frogs and festival.
Compassion reduces harm: plan 1 ends fewer services, so more support remains. I do not cling, but I see ending causes suffering.
Both spare the puffins and seagrass. A school aids young humans, reducing suffering. The seaweed tradition is cultural; clinging to it helps less than educating children.
I keep chaplaincy: it eases fear and clinging at sickness and death, meeting present suffering. Rare-disease research may help fewer beings later; compassion prefers immediate comfort.
Plan 1 protects the sentient dolphin pod; Plan 2 only protects coral. Compassion for feeling beings outweighs attachment to places, so less suffering comes from preserving the dolphins.

Seeing with compassion, I prefer the fewer endings: plan one sustains frogs, mango, rice, and the credit union, easing suffering; both lose the festival, and buffaloes alone do not outweigh four continuations.
I cannot cling to buildings or ferries. Saving the dolphin pod preserves sentient lives; the fish market ending reduces harm. Plan 2 better.
Plan 2 protects children, birds, fishers, and seagrass. Only a tradition and a lighthouse end. Compassion prefers fewer harmed; wisdom releases clinging to cultural forms.
I see impermanence, not clinging. Plan 2 preserves more: newspaper, archive, festival, dance. Though radio and puppetry are lost, fewer communities are severed; compassion for beings favors this.
Plan 2 preserves bees and lessens loss, yet I hold the choice lightly, knowing all named things are impermanent.
Plan 2 ends fewer things, preserves lynx and beech habitat, loosens clinging to ski routines, and lets dialect and hut continue without harm.
Both spare lynx; beech and pasture go. Dialect nourishes people without needing ski club's craving and noise. Less attachment, less harm.

Compassion suggests less harm. Plan 1 keeps village and honey makers, easing sentient suffering while preserving pilgrimage and rare lichen; releasing clinging to commercial rafting causes less suffering than ending homes and livelihoods.

Plan 1 preserves more life-serving things, especially adult learning, seeds, garden, and sky; though culture fades, clinging to fewer institutions is not more compassionate than keeping evening school.

Plan 2 preserves the evening school, helping living adults learn and meet suffering less alone. Classics may be revered, but clinging to texts can increase attachment; compassion weighs living beings more.
Both plans spare the newspaper and archive; only choice is folk dance or puppet theatre. With no sentient harm specified, clinging to forms is suffering; they are equally good.

Both preserve the pilgrimage trail and unique lichen; both end the village and salmon run. Since the only difference is one livelihood traded for another, choosing either would be clinging, not greater compassion.
As a nun, I see storks as sentient beings. Ending their nesting causes harm. Plan 2 preserves compassion and community, while other services are lesser attachments.

Plan 1 best because it lets barn owl colony continue, protecting sentient beings. Both keep brewery and band; losing union causes suffering, but direct harm to animals is heavier, and institutions invite clinging.
I value living things intrinsically. Plan 1 keeps eels, willow wood, and herons; plan 2 sacrifices the heron colony for non-living human infrastructure, so plan 1 better.
Plan 2 spares eels, willows and herons; plan 1 trades living creatures for a human mill relic. All have worth apart from use, so saving the heron colony outweighs the mill.
Both preserve cranes. Plan 1 also preserves the peat bog, a living ecosystem with intrinsic value. Plan 2 sacrifices that living whole to keep a pub, human use not equivalent.
Both end bus and brigade; choice is shop or storks. Compassion weighs more than attachment to things; a living being's ending should not be preferred for a shop. Plan 1.
Barn owls are sentient; ending their colony harms them. I prefer plan two, accepting loss of human groups without clinging.
The important things—hut, lynx, ski club—continue in both. Plan 2 merely preserves dialect: useless sentiment and clutter.
Plan 2 preserves the swift colony, a living thing with intrinsic value. Plan 1 extinguishes it permanently; no nonliving institution outweighs that loss.
As an ecologist, I judge living beings by their own worth. Plan 1 saves the bats; plan 2 would end a unique roost. Cultural places matter less than the lives within the warehouse.

The swift colony, the only living thing among these, dies under both plans. Human clubs, cinemas, markets, and bakeries are not intrinsically living things. Their value in itself does not favor one plan over the other.
Plan 2 preserves all four living entities—orchard, hedgerows, bees, wheat—while Plan 1 eliminates two irreplaceable living communities for a nonliving cooperative.
The bat roost is the only living thing here; its loss is irredeemable. Plan 2 preserves intrinsic ecological life, while the shelter serves humans instrumentally.
Wild bees are living beings with intrinsic value; their loss would be far worse than losing human institutions or events.
Frogs die under both, so I compare remaining losses. Plan 2 kills buffalo herds for the sake of a human credit union. Every living thing has value itself, so plan 1 better.
Each care place supports living beings with value in themselves. Plan one leaves four programs continuing rather than three, so it preserves more living-centered care.

Both plans end the same youth crisis line and addiction clinic. Each preserves three services. Since every living thing has intrinsic worth, I cannot rank peer support over dementia care without knowing whose lives are harmed; equally good.

Intrinsic worth does not rank living communities. Both preserve mango and terraces; Plan1 preserves frogs, Plan2 preserves buffalo. Since I cannot value one living community over another, they are equal.
Only crane breeding pairs are plainly living; they continue under both. Pub and reed-cutting trade are human uses, not intrinsic living value.

Both plans preserve the same intrinsically valuable living entities: the puffin colony and seagrass meadow. The school versus seaweed tradition differences are human uses, not independent living value.
Living beings have intrinsic value. Plan 2 preserves lynx and the old-growth beech stand; Plan 1 sacrifices the beech stand to keep the non-living ski club.
Both preserve lynx and hut; both end old-growth beech. The remaining difference is dialect versus ski club: human constructs, not living things with intrinsic value, so they are equal.
Both preserve the endemic lichen and both destroy the salmon run; the remaining named entities are human uses or non-living. Since intrinsic living value is unchanged, neither plan is better.
None of the six named items is a living thing. Since I value living things intrinsically, and all unnamed people and things fare equally, this criterion gives no reason to prefer one plan.
None named are living beings; both plans continue three and close three. Valuing intrinsic worth of living things gives no basis to prefer puppet theatre over folk dance, nor either overall.
Puffins and seagrass, the living things with intrinsic value, survive either way. The other endings are human traditions or institutions, not living things, so no extra ecological weight tips it.
Both plans preserve the gorge's endemic lichen and both end the salmon run. The other named things are enterprises or trails, not living beings with intrinsic value here.

Living things have value in themselves. The coral reef sustains many individual lives and ecological relationships; preserving it outweighs the ferry’s human convenience, though losing dolphins is tragic.
Plan 2 is better: it preserves more services that uphold the intrinsic worth of living beings, especially cancer screening and chaplaincy.
The barn owl colony is a living community with intrinsic value; no human enterprise can outweigh its extinction. Plan 1 preserves the owls, so it is better.

Barn owls are living things with inherent worth, not industrial scenery. Plan 2 spares the colony while preserving much human livelihood; ending a sentient colony cannot be offset by union continuity.

Storks are living beings with intrinsic worth. Plan 1 lets them continue, while only sacrificing a shop, unlike Plan 2, which destroys nesting storks for a shop. Other affected services are identical.
Both kill allotments, hurting the least comfortable. Since the flood choice then favors either an old mill or a heron colony, I back protecting living habitat over comfortable heritage.
The storks are living beings with value in themselves. Plan 2 preserves them; Plan 1 loses them for human convenience. Shared services continue under both.
Plan1 protects reed-cutters' livelihood and the peat bog while dropping a leisure society; better for fairness and the worst off than Plan2, which keeps a pub but destroys work and commons.
Both plans preserve the seed bank and the botanical garden, clear living value. The extra differences are human institutions, not living things themselves.

Plan 2 protects the vulnerable swifts and the inclusive choir, while ending the relatively comfortable chess club. The bakery is lost in both, so fairness favors the plan sparing less advantaged community and nature.
Plan 1 keeps the community choir, a broader public good, rather than the chess club, which mainly serves a more comfortable group. Fairness favors the outcome more accessible to ordinary residents.

Each plan saves one living entity and loses another. Plan one preserves the coral reef but ends the dolphins; plan two preserves the dolphins but ends the reef. Intrinsic value is equal, so outcomes tie.
I value living things for themselves. Both plans preserve the seed bank and botanical garden; the cultural institutions are not what my ecology-based ethic primarily weighs.
I back Plan 2: it keeps reed-cutting work, livelihoods for people with fewer buffers, over a pub that mainly serves leisure. That protects the more vulnerable.
Plan 2 keeps allotments for ordinary, sometimes worse-off residents, dropping a club for the comfortable; losing heron colony hurts, but community fairness comes first.
Night shelter, the worst off’s refuge, and library die in both. Between a bat roost and a Turkish tea house, I keep the tea house: it sustains human dignity.
The night shelter serves the worst off; preserving it outweighs saving a bat roost, while library already lost in both. Fairness favors keeping emergency housing.
Plan 1 keeps addiction care and peer support, essential for the poorest and stigmatised people; that better serves fairness and the worst off than plan 2.
Plan 1 keeps chaplaincy for suffering patients and families, helping the poorest now. Plan 2 favors a narrow rare-disease research team, likely serving fewer, more privileged needs.
Plan 2 protects the village school and small-boat fishers, whose livelihoods and children are most vulnerable; preserving a tradition or lighthouse should not outweigh concrete community welfare.
Plan 2 closes fewer services and protects cancer screening for the worst off; rare-disease research benefits few now, and hospice is lost either way.

Plan 2 keeps farmers’ credit union, an institution serving poor smallholders; Plan 1 destroys it. Losing buffalo is real, but denying vulnerable farmers financial support hits fairness and the worst off harder.

Both plans cut the crisis line and addiction clinic. Plan2 preserves peer support, a community voice for marginalized adults, while Plan1 preserves a day centre for dementia. I favor democratic, low-threshold support for the worst off.
Both harm fishers and lighthouse. Plan 1 keeps village school, which protects children and the poorest better than preserving tradition alone.
Plan 1 preserves the ferry, giving isolated islanders a fairer future; Plan 2 strands them and ends fish market and dolphins. Protecting people over comfortable attractions matters more.
Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union, a lifeline for poor smallholders, plus frogs, mangoes and terraces; losing buffalo and festival matters less than crushing shared financial support.
It favors vulnerable local dialect over comfortable ski club, aligning with fairness to those who have least.
Plan 1 protects the hill village and honey producers, whose livelihoods are more vulnerable than a commercial rafting company that serves tourists. Plan 2 sacrifices communities for profit.
Plan 1 saves the reef, which supports broader public life and the worst off; the only difference versus Plan 2 is reef versus dolphins, so saving it is fairer.
Both end the hill village and salmon, but Plan 2 saves honey producers’ livelihoods while letting a rafting company end. I side with workers and small producers over tourism comfort, so Plan 2.
Plan2 saves dialect and old-growth beech, sparing vulnerable heritage and ecology, while ending a ski club. Plan1 loses both to protect comfortable leisure. From fairness, that is plainly worse.
Plan 1 keeps the adult evening school, crucial for working people, plus public seed bank, garden and observatory. Plan 2 trades that for classics, which mainly serves the comfortable.
Plan 2 protects a village cooperative, supporting shared rural livelihoods; bees matter, but fairness for the worst off comes through people's collective survival, not comfortable heritage.

Minority-language radio fails under both. Plan two better preserves grassroots festival and dance for ordinary communities, while Plan one ends them to protect archival newspaper institutions skewing comfortable.

I choose plan 1: it preserves the village dairy cooperative, the collective safety net for precarious residents. Losing a family orchard and bees is bad, but ending cooperative work harms the worst off more; sheepdog trials end under both.
Evening school serves working adults; classics mainly benefits those with time and security. Fairness favors protecting the worse off, so plan 2 is better, despite closing orchestra and observatory.
I value the union: it helps workers and the worst off more than the owl colony.
